If the realized assignment is \((1,0)\), we observe the entire second row of this transposed table: outcomes 3 and 5. We do not observe one person’s outcome from the all-treated world and the other’s from the all-control world. This is the first change in how we should read experimental data under interference.
The other component of SUTVA matters too. “Use the new recommendation algorithm” is incomplete if its training data change with the experiment’s allocation. One can expand the intervention to include the training protocol and thereby obtain well-defined potential outcomes, but that expansion does not restore no interference. A precise intervention and the absence of spillovers are separate requirements.
crumbs: 7  L05: Interference

title: L05: Interference
text:
Four mechanisms that create interference
The mechanisms below produce different scientific questions. They also suggest different restrictions on \(Y_i(\mathbf z)\). The displayed functions are illustrative models developed for these notes, not claims that the cited applications obey an exact equation.
Social interaction. A reminder can affect its recipient and, through conversation, the recipient’s friends. Bond et al. (2012) studied political mobilization through an online social network. The distinction between receiving a message and being connected to its recipients is central to this setting. Let \(A_{ij}\) indicate a pretreatment social connection from \(j\) to \(i\). A simple model is
\[
Y_i(\mathbf z)
=a_i+b_i z_i+\sum_{j\ne i}A_{ij}c_{ij}z_j.
\tag{2}\]
Here \(a_i\) is the baseline outcome, \(b_i\) the own-treatment contribution, and \(c_{ij}\) the contribution of treating a connected person. These coefficients are fixed, and the equation is a restriction on the science table. It is not a regression fitted to the observed cross-section. Social reinforcement could also generate interactions such as \(z_jz_k\), so additivity is a substantive simplification.
Markets. Two sellers can compete for the same buyer even if they never communicate. A treatment that makes one listing more attractive can divert demand from another. Holtz et al. (2024) use a pricing meta-experiment on Airbnb to study this kind of interference. For a small illustration, let two sellers divide one unit of demand, and let \(\delta>0\) measure the increase in a seller’s attractiveness under treatment:
\[
Y_1(z_1,z_2)=\frac{\exp(\delta z_1)}{\exp(\delta z_1)+\exp(\delta z_2)},
\qquad Y_2(z_1,z_2)=1-Y_1(z_1,z_2).
\]
A treated seller outperforms an untreated competitor. Yet changing both sellers’ treatment leaves both market shares at one half. An individual advantage can therefore coexist with zero change in average market share under universal adoption. For revenues or welfare, total demand might also change; that would require a different response function. Calling a treatment successful requires specifying which market outcome and which policy comparison matter.
Spatial movement. A local restriction can shift activity across a border. Chang et al. (2023) study spillovers in mobility under California’s county-level COVID-19 restrictions using a regression-discontinuity design. Their application is observational; it illustrates the mechanism, while our subsequent analysis concerns randomized assignments. A stylized county outcome could depend on both its own policy and neighboring policies:
\[
Y_i(\mathbf z)
=a_i-b_i z_i+\sum_{j\ne i}w_{ij}z_j,
\qquad w_{ij}\geq0.
\]
Own restrictions reduce local activity, whereas restrictions elsewhere can redirect activity toward county \(i\). The weights might reflect travel connections rather than geographic adjacency. Restricting one county and restricting an entire region are distinct interventions even for a resident whose own county has the same policy in both cases.
Shared learning and symbiosis bias. A recommendation algorithm learns from the behavior it induces. If two experimental algorithms share those data, one can benefit from exploration performed by the other. Brennan et al. (2025) study the resulting discrepancy between mixed-algorithm experiments and separate deployment. Let \(D_t(\mathbf z)\) denote the training data accumulated before period \(t\) under allocation \(\mathbf z\), and let \(\theta_{a,t}(\mathbf z)\) be the fitted state of algorithm \(a\in\{0,1\}\). A schematic representation is
\[
\theta_{a,t}(\mathbf z)=\mathcal A_a\{D_t(\mathbf z)\},
\qquad
Y_{it}(\mathbf z)=g_i\{z_i,\theta_{z_i,t}(\mathbf z)\}.
\]
The symbol \(\mathcal A_a\) denotes the algorithm’s training procedure. Although user \(i\) interacts with one algorithm, its trained state depends on other users’ assignments. Separating training data can reduce this channel, but also changes the quantity of data available to each algorithm. That intervention may itself differ from full deployment. The system being evaluated includes the learning process, not just a fixed scoring rule.
These examples are not exhausted by a friendship graph. A graph used in design should represent a plausible channel of causal influence: competition, mobility, shared learning, or social interaction. A convenient data structure alone is not evidence that all interference follows its edges.
crumbs: 7  L05: Interference

title: L05: Interference
text:
Which treatment effect?

Universal adoption and individual treatment
For a decision about deployment to everyone, the natural finite-population target is
\[
\tau_{\mathrm G}
=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N
\{Y_i(\mathbf 1_N)-Y_i(\mathbf 0_N)\}.
\tag{3}\]
The vectors \(\mathbf 1_N\) and \(\mathbf 0_N\) assign everyone to treatment and control, respectively. We call \(\tau_{\mathrm G}\) the global average treatment effect (GATE); “total treatment effect” is another name used for this deployment contrast. It includes the consequences of treating the unit and of changing its environment. In the two-user table, it equals \(\{(5-2)+(8-4)\}/2=3.5\).
Now independently treat each unit with probability \(p\in(0,1)\). The ordinary individual-treatment HT contrast is
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{own}}
=\frac1N\sum_i
\left\{\frac{Z_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{p}
-\frac{(1-Z_i)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{1-p}\right\}.
\]
Its expectation can still be calculated exactly. Conditioning first on the other units’ assignments, independence gives
\[
\mathbb E_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{own}})
=\frac1N\sum_i\mathbb E_{Z_{-i}}
\{Y_i(1,\mathbf Z_{-i})-Y_i(0,\mathbf Z_{-i})\}
\equiv\tau_D(p).
\tag{4}\]
Here \(\mathbf Z_{-i}\) is the vector with unit \(i\) removed, and \(Y_i(a,\mathbf Z_{-i})\) places \(a\) in position \(i\). The expectation averages over independent Bernoulli-\(p\) assignments to the others. Thus \(\tau_D(p)\) changes one’s own treatment while averaging over the same distribution of other people’s treatments on both sides. It is a design-specific average direct effect, not generally the universal-adoption contrast.
In the two-user example, \(\tau_D(p)=(1+3)/2=2\) for every \(p\). The difference from 3.5 is the average spillover contribution, 1.5. In other response functions, own-treatment effects interact with others’ treatments and \(\tau_D(p)\) itself changes with \(p\). Neither randomization nor inverse-probability weighting says these two estimands must coincide.
This calculation uses independent assignment. Under complete randomization, conditioning on a unit being treated leaves fewer treatments available for its peers than conditioning on it being a control. One must use the actual conditional assignment laws. The design is part of the interpretation of an individual-treatment contrast under interference.


Exposure mappings compress the science table
A messaging feature may depend on the assignments of a person’s close contacts but not on assignments elsewhere. Or only the number of treated contacts may matter, rather than their identities. These are different restrictions, and exposure mappings give a language for stating them (Aronow and Samii 2017).
For each unit, an exposure mapping is a specified function
\[
f_i:\{0,1\}^N\longrightarrow\mathcal E_i,
\qquad E_i=f_i(\mathbf Z),
\]
where \(\mathcal E_i\) is the set of possible exposure labels. The substantive assumption is that assignments receiving the same label produce the same outcome:
\[
f_i(\mathbf z)=f_i(\mathbf z')
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Y_i(\mathbf z)=Y_i(\mathbf z').
\tag{5}\]
We can then write the common outcome as \(y_i(e)\) for exposure \(e\). Lowercase \(y_i(e)\) distinguishes an exposure-indexed outcome from \(Y_i(\mathbf z)\), the original assignment-indexed function. The mapping is an assumption about equality among cells of the science table. Computing it from observed assignments does not establish that the equality holds.
Let \(G\) be a fixed, pretreatment, undirected interference graph. Write \(\mathcal N_i\) for the closed neighborhood of \(i\): the unit itself and its neighbors. Its size is \(d_i=|\mathcal N_i|\). A local-interference model says that \(Y_i(\mathbf z)\) depends only on the subvector \(\mathbf z_{\mathcal N_i}\). This permits arbitrary interactions among neighbors’ assignments. A more restrictive mapping uses own treatment and the fraction of other neighbors treated:
\[
f_i(\mathbf z)=(z_i,q_i(\mathbf z)),
\qquad
q_i(\mathbf z)=\frac{1}{d_i-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i\setminus\{i\}}z_j,
\]
with \(q_i=0\) for an isolated unit. Equal fractions now imply equal outcomes even when different neighbors are treated. A close friend and a distant acquaintance become interchangeable for this purpose. That is additional modeling, not a consequence of locality.
For GATE estimation, two exposure conditions have a special role. Unit \(i\) is network exposed to treatment if its observed outcome equals \(Y_i(\mathbf 1_N)\), and network exposed to control if it equals \(Y_i(\mathbf 0_N)\). Under the local-interference model, sufficient observable conditions are
\[
E_i=e_1:\ z_j=1\text{ for every }j\in\mathcal N_i,
\qquad
E_i=e_0:\ z_j=0\text{ for every }j\in\mathcal N_i.
\tag{6}\]
These are full-neighborhood exposures (Ugander et al. 2013). They allow a local part of a mixed experiment to reveal an outcome from a global counterfactual. The outcome may vary arbitrarily among mixed neighborhoods; we need not pool all mixed assignments into one outcome-equivalent category. Threshold or fractional exposure rules can make the extreme labels more common, but identifying them with global outcomes then requires stronger substantive assumptions.
There are other ways to restrict the science table. An exposure model equates outcomes under different assignments. A low-order response model instead restricts how treatment indicators combine algebraically, potentially allowing every assignment to have a distinct outcome. L06 develops that alternative. Neither approach obtains its assumptions from randomization alone.


Moving SUTVA to clusters
Sometimes a plausible grouping is available before specifying a network: households, schools, or geographically isolated villages. Let \(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_K\}\) be a partition and \(c(i)\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\) the index of the cluster containing unit \(i\). Partial interference assumes that
\[
\mathbf z_{C_{c(i)}}=\mathbf z'_{C_{c(i)}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Y_i(\mathbf z)=Y_i(\mathbf z').
\tag{7}\]
Assignments within the cluster can interact arbitrarily; assignments outside it do not affect \(i\). Hudgens and Halloran (2008) develop effects and designs in this setting. Karrer et al.’s network-experimentation paper, first circulated in 2020, calls this SUTVA for clusters (Karrer et al. 2021). It is a restriction on the interference structure, not an automatic consequence of assigning treatments by cluster. Candogan, Chen, and Niazadeh (2024) also use no interference across clusters when optimizing correlations among cluster assignments. This connects cluster SUTVA to an established literature on partial interference and to subsequent work on experimental design.
If each cluster receives a single treatment \(W_k\), the allowed unit assignments satisfy \(Z_i=W_{c(i)}\). On this restricted set of assignments, partial interference implies that the outcome depends only on \(W_{c(i)}\). Cluster totals can then be analyzed as potential outcomes indexed by one cluster treatment, with size weighting if the target averages over individuals.
There is a useful distinction between requiring partial interference for every conceivable assignment and requiring this invariance only on the design’s cluster-constant assignments. For example, suppose units 3 and 4 form another cluster and \(Y_1(\mathbf z)=z_1+z_3-z_4\). Cross-cluster interference exists when units 3 and 4 receive different treatments. Under a design that always assigns them together, their effects cancel. The restricted experiment therefore has a cluster-level invariance that the unrestricted science table lacks. This example illustrates a distinction between assumption domains; it is not a new definition attributed to Karrer et al.
Cluster SUTVA can be operationally useful without committing to a detailed exposure mapping within each cluster. Mathematically, however, it can itself be expressed as a mapping that retains the cluster’s treatment vector. Exposure mappings and cluster SUTVA are therefore overlapping ways to express restrictions, not mutually exclusive causal frameworks.

title: L05: Interference
section: From observed exposures to an estimator
text:
From observed exposures to an estimator

The inverse probability is now an exposure probability
Suppose the mapping is adequate for exposures \(e_1\) and \(e_0\), so that \(y_i(e_a)=Y_i(a\mathbf 1_N)\) for \(a\in\{0,1\}\). Define the marginal and joint exposure probabilities under the chosen design by
\[
\pi_i(e)=\mathbb P_Z(E_i=e),
\qquad
\pi_{ij}(e,e')=\mathbb P_Z(E_i=e,E_j=e').
\]
These probabilities average over assignments, holding the graph and potential outcomes fixed. They are not estimated observational propensity scores. A unit can have treatment probability one half and an exceedingly small probability of experiencing an all-treated neighborhood.
If both required exposures have positive probability for every unit, define
\[
\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}(e)
=\frac1N\sum_i\frac{\mathbf 1\{E_i=e\}Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\pi_i(e)},
\qquad
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{G,HT}}
=\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}(e_1)-\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}(e_0).
\tag{8}\]

Proposition 1 (Design unbiasedness under an adequate exposure model) If exposure \(e_a\) reveals \(Y_i(a\mathbf 1_N)\) and \(\pi_i(e_a)>0\) for every \(i\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}\), then \(\mathbb E_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{G,HT}})=\tau_{\mathrm G}\).


Proof. On the event \(E_i=e_a\), consistency and the exposure assumption replace the observed outcome by the fixed number \(Y_i(a\mathbf 1_N)\). Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E_Z\left\{
\frac{\mathbf 1\{E_i=e_a\}Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\pi_i(e_a)}
\right\}
=\frac{\pi_i(e_a)Y_i(a\mathbf 1_N)}{\pi_i(e_a)}
=Y_i(a\mathbf 1_N).
\]
Average over units and subtract the control expression. No independence among exposures is used.

The familiar HT cancellation survives interference. What changes is the event that makes a particular potential outcome observable. Weighting cannot repair a misspecified exposure model: if different assignments with label \(e_1\) produce different outcomes, the weighted average targets their design-weighted mean, which need not equal the all-treated outcome.
A Hájek version divides the weighted outcome sum by the weighted count of units in that exposure. As in L02, this can improve stability, but exact design unbiasedness is generally lost and a zero denominator must be handled. Choosing normalization does not resolve an incorrect mapping or zero exposure probability.


Positivity and joint observability
Under independent Bernoulli-\(p\) unit assignment and full-neighborhood exposure,
\[
\pi_i(e_1)=p^{d_i},
\qquad
\pi_i(e_0)=(1-p)^{d_i}.
\tag{9}\]
Each of the \(d_i\) assignments must agree. At \(p=1/2\), a closed neighborhood of size 11 receives either particular extreme exposure with probability \(1/2048\). A large experiment can contain many treated units but very few observations of the outcomes needed for its deployment target. This is L04’s weak-positivity problem created by the combination of network structure, estimand, and design.
The pairwise probabilities matter for inference. Write \(s_{e_1}=1\) and \(s_{e_0}=-1\). Expanding the variance of Equation 8 gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{G,HT}})
=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}\sum_{e,e'\in\{e_1,e_0\}}
s_es_{e'}
\frac{\pi_{ij}(e,e')-\pi_i(e)\pi_j(e')}
{\pi_i(e)\pi_j(e')}
y_i(e)y_j(e').
\tag{10}\]
For \(i=j\), interpret the joint probability in the usual way: it equals \(\pi_i(e)\) if \(e=e'\) and zero otherwise. The formula follows by writing the estimator as a sum of weighted indicators and using the covariance of each pair. It displays both rare-exposure weights and dependence among exposures.
Even when each marginal probability is positive, some joint probabilities are zero. If two closed neighborhoods overlap, one cannot simultaneously be all treated and the other all control. The corresponding product of potential outcomes is never jointly observed. It cannot be estimated by dividing an observed product by its joint probability. Conservative variance procedures handle these unidentified terms with bounds; normal approximations additionally require an appropriate sequence of growing experiments and restrictions on dependence (Aronow and Samii 2017). An ordinary independent-observation standard error ignores precisely the structure that made interference relevant.

title: L05: Interference
text:
Testing whether interference is present
An assumption can be useful without being beyond scrutiny. Testing interference requires care because “no interference” still permits each unit to have an unknown direct treatment effect. We must preserve that uncertainty while finding assignments under which the relevant outcomes can be imputed.

Make the null sharp on a conditional experiment
The global sharp null \(Y_i(\mathbf z)=Y_i(\mathbf z')\) for every \(i,\mathbf z,\mathbf z'\) rules out all treatment effects. Rejecting it does not specifically establish interference: ordinary direct effects suffice. The no-interference null in Equation 1 is weaker. It supplies no value for a treated person’s outcome under their own control assignment.
The conditional-testing approach of Athey, Eckles, and Imbens (2018) makes the null sharp for selected focal units by restricting the assignments considered. Choose a set \(F\) of focal units before seeing treatment or outcomes, for example using only the pretreatment graph. Condition on their realized own assignments \(\mathbf Z_F\). Under no interference, their outcomes are then fixed for every reassignment of the remaining, auxiliary units.
To see a statistic one could use, let \(q_i(\mathbf z)\) be the treated-neighbor fraction defined earlier, and let \(\overline Y_F^{\mathrm{obs}}\) be the mean focal outcome. Consider
\[
T(\mathbf z)
=\sum_{i\in F}(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-\overline Y_F^{\mathrm{obs}})
\left[q_i(\mathbf z)-
\mathbb E_Z\{q_i(\mathbf Z)\mid\mathbf Z_F\}\right].
\]
The outcome factors stay fixed. The exposure factors vary as auxiliary treatments are reassigned. Positive values indicate that focal outcomes tend to be larger where randomized neighbor exposure is larger. A two-sided test could use \(|T|\).
The reference distribution must be the actual conditional design, \(\mathbb P_Z(\mathbf Z_{-F}\mid\mathbf Z_F)\). Under independent Bernoulli assignment, auxiliary assignments remain independent with probability \(p\). Under complete randomization, the number of auxiliary treatments is fixed by the original treatment budget and the observed focal assignments. Simply flipping independent coins would analyze the wrong experiment in the latter case.
Conditional on \(\mathbf Z_F\), the observed assignment and a fresh draw from this conditional law have the same distribution under the null, while every outcome entering the statistic is known. Ranking the observed statistic in this distribution therefore gives a valid randomization \(p\)-value, with discreteness handled conservatively. For Monte Carlo sampling, including the observed allocation in the usual plus-one construction avoids zero estimated \(p\)-values.
This argument does not require the chosen neighbor statistic to describe the actual interference correctly. Under the null there is no interference to describe. A poor graph or statistic reduces power, whereas an incorrect conditional assignment law can invalidate the test. Choosing focal units after observing assignments is possible, but requires conditioning on the selection mechanism as well; selecting favorable focal units and then pretending they were fixed is not justified.


Randomize the randomization mechanism
A different strategy deliberately creates different local environments at the same marginal treatment probability. Saveski et al. (2017) compare individual and cluster randomization within a randomized meta-experiment. The outer randomization allocates groups to the two experimental strategies; the inner randomization assigns treatment according to each strategy. Under no interference, both strategies target the same average direct effect. Their discrepancy can reveal interference without requiring an exact spillover model.
For a concrete design-based version, let \(R_i\in\{0,1\}\) record the strategy to which unit \(i\) is assigned, with known probability \(\rho_i(r)=\mathbb P(R_i=r)\). Suppose each strategy gives that unit conditional treatment probability \(p\). An HT contrast for strategy \(r\) is
\[
\widehat\tau_r
=\frac1N\sum_i\frac{\mathbf 1\{R_i=r\}}{\rho_i(r)}
\left\{\frac{Z_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{p}
-\frac{(1-Z_i)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{1-p}\right\}.
\]
Under no interference, iterated expectation over the outer and inner assignments gives \(\mathbb E(\widehat\tau_r)=N^{-1}\sum_i\{Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\}\) for both strategies. Hence \(\widehat\tau_1-\widehat\tau_0\) is centered at zero. This calculation explains the role of randomizing strategy membership: the comparison is not confounded by choosing different populations for the two designs. Its variance must incorporate both randomizations and their covariances.
Under interference, cluster assignment makes own treatment more correlated with neighbors’ treatments. In the two-user example, assigning both users together produces the global contrast 3.5, whereas independent assignment produces the direct-effect contrast 2. A strategy comparison can detect this discrepancy. For a real network with edges crossing clusters, neither strategy need identify GATE. The test compares the effects revealed by the two designs; it does not certify one as unbiased for universal deployment. Nonrejection likewise does not establish no interference, because the designs can miss relevant channels or have little power.


Use randomized increases in treatment allocation
Platforms often expand a treatment gradually. A control unit that remains untreated can experience an increasingly treated environment. Han, Li, Mao, and Wu (2023) use increasing-allocation experiments to test for cross-unit interference. The useful variation is in other units’ randomized treatment histories, rather than a raw comparison of outcomes at different dates.
Consider two periods with marginal treatment probabilities \(p_1<p_2\). Draw independent \(U_i\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) and set \(Z_{it}=\mathbf 1\{U_i\leq p_t\}\). Each unit’s treatment history is one of \((0,0)\), \((0,1)\), or \((1,1)\), with probabilities \(1-p_2\), \(p_2-p_1\), and \(p_1\). The history \((1,0)\) is impossible. Write \(Y_{it}(\mathbf z_{1:2})\) for the potential outcome when the full two-period assignment matrix is specified. The no-cross-unit-interference null says that this outcome depends only on unit \(i\)’s own treatment history. It can still depend on time and on that own history.
A conditional experiment can hold focal units’ entire treatment histories fixed and randomize the auxiliary histories. For example, preselect a focal set \(F\) using the graph and condition on the histories of every unit in this original set. Within the statistic, use only focal units whose own assignment is unchanged, and form \(\Delta Y_i=Y_{i2}^{\mathrm{obs}}-Y_{i1}^{\mathrm{obs}}\). These differences are fixed under the null after conditioning on focal histories. A statistic can associate \(\Delta Y_i\) with the change in treated-neighbor fraction, \(q_i(\mathbf Z_2)-q_i(\mathbf Z_1)\). Focal units that switch treatment remain conditioned upon even though their outcomes do not enter this statistic; they do not move into the auxiliary pool.
Conditional on the counts of histories among units outside the original \(F\), iid rollout assignment makes those auxiliary histories exchangeable. Permuting whole histories only among units outside \(F\) preserves both the rollout and this conditional law. Recompute neighbor exposures after each permutation and compare the observed statistic with the resulting distribution. Separately permuting the two treatment columns could create forbidden \((1,0)\) histories and would not reproduce the design.
Differencing can help remove persistent unit differences from the statistic; its validity here does not require all time trends to be common because focal outcomes are held fixed under the null. Tests that instead exchange periods, or interpret a changing treatment-control contrast as evidence by itself, require additional restrictions. The paper also develops a more powerful procedure under a time-fixed-effect model. That additional model is consequential: seasonality, changing treatment effects, or carryover can otherwise resemble an allocation effect.
The three strategies use distinct sources of variation. Conditional tests hold own treatment fixed while varying others’ assignments. Meta-experiments vary the mechanism assigning treatment. Rollouts vary treatment histories across time. In each case, valid inference follows from an explicit assignment or invariance argument; the visual appearance of spillovers is only a starting point.

title: L05: Interference
text:
Designing for informative exposures
Testing can reveal that individual randomization answers an incomplete policy question. The next design question is how to make the desired exposures occur more often while retaining enough independent comparisons.

Graph cluster randomization
For a fixed partition \(\mathcal C\), assign cluster treatments \(W_1,\ldots,W_K\) independently as Bernoulli-\(p\), and set \(Z_i=W_{c(i)}\). Let \(k_i(\mathcal C)\) be the number of distinct clusters intersecting the closed neighborhood \(\mathcal N_i\). Then full-neighborhood exposure probabilities are
\[
\pi_i(e_1\mid\mathcal C)=p^{k_i(\mathcal C)},
\qquad
\pi_i(e_0\mid\mathcal C)=(1-p)^{k_i(\mathcal C)}.
\tag{11}\]
Only the assignments of these clusters must agree. The number of independent choices in the exponent can be much smaller than the number of units. This is the central mechanism of graph cluster randomization (GCR) (Ugander et al. 2013). It does not require there to be no edges across clusters: an exposure estimator can account for those edges when calculating the events and their probabilities.
Take a path of six units, \(1-2-3-4-5-6\), and \(p=1/2\). Under individual randomization, each endpoint has closed-neighborhood size two and each interior unit size three. Group the path into clusters \(\{1,2,3\}\) and \(\{4,5,6\}\).

Interior units away from the cut benefit most. Units 3 and 4 remain near a cluster boundary and require both clusters to agree. The calculation makes clear why counting the number of cut edges alone need not describe every unit’s statistical difficulty.
Larger clusters can increase these marginal probabilities but also increase dependence. With one cluster containing the entire graph, every unit receives an extreme exposure, yet there is only one randomized treatment coin. The observed data are either the whole all-treated population or the whole all-control population. HT remains unbiased across repeated experiments, but the two worlds are never observed together. Exposure frequency and precision are different objectives.
For unequal clusters, one must also distinguish averaging people from averaging clusters. The unweighted mean of cluster means targets an average cluster, giving a person in a small cluster more weight. An estimator of Equation 3 must preserve the intended individual weights.


Randomize the clustering too
In a fixed clustering, some units repeatedly occupy favorable interiors and others unfavorable boundaries. Randomized graph cluster randomization (RGCR) draws a partition from a specified distribution \(Q\), then randomizes cluster treatments. Ugander and Yin (2023) study this design and randomized graph-decomposition algorithms, with variance guarantees under graph-structure assumptions.
The two-stage exposure probability is
\[
\pi_i(e_1)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal C\sim Q}
\{p^{k_i(\mathcal C)}\},
\qquad
\pi_i(e_0)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal C\sim Q}
\{(1-p)^{k_i(\mathcal C)}\}.
\tag{12}\]
The expectation is over the random partition. For example, if a unit’s neighborhood touches one cluster half the time and three clusters half the time, its treatment-exposure probability at \(p=1/2\) is \((1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/8)=5/16\). It is not permanently assigned the unfavorable probability \(1/8\).
One simple partition construction gives units independent continuous random priorities and assigns each unit to the highest-priority vertex in its closed neighborhood; equal chosen vertices define a cluster. This is the 1-hop-max construction. Its purpose is to make cluster membership vary through local random choices while remaining tied to graph proximity. The resulting clusters are then independently treated or controlled.
An exposure estimator using the marginal probabilities in Equation 12 is unbiased over both randomizations. It need not be unbiased conditional on the realized partition. Using conditional probabilities instead defines another estimator, with conditional unbiasedness when those probabilities are positive. The analyst must match the probability in the denominator to the randomization distribution used for the claimed result.
Monte Carlo computation can approximate the marginal probabilities by repeatedly drawing partitions. This is design simulation and does not require outcomes. However, replacing a probability by a noisy estimate inside its reciprocal does not preserve exact unbiasedness. Rare exposures require accurate probability calculations and enough simulations; increasing the number of outcome units does not automatically eliminate probability-computation error.

title: L05: Interference
section: A clustering is optimal for an objective
text:
A clustering is optimal for an objective
Community detection seeks a descriptive partition of a network. Experimental design asks which partition makes an estimator accurate for a specified causal target. These problems can overlap, but their objectives need not agree.
Viviano et al. (2026) study clustering for the particular assignment-weighted contrast
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathcal C}
=\frac{2}{N}\sum_i(2Z_i-1)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}},
\tag{13}\]
under independent fair cluster assignment. The fixed denominator is \(N\), not a realized treatment-arm count. This estimator weights own treatment, rather than requiring full-neighborhood exposure, and can be biased for GATE when clusters exchange spillovers. Their framework chooses clusters by a worst-case bias-variance criterion over a restricted class of potential outcomes, leading to a penalized graph-cut optimization. The result is therefore about an estimator, target, design class, and response class together. It is not a claim that a single partition is optimal for all analyses.
An additive calculation shows why this criterion has a different form from maximizing exposure probabilities. Use Equation 2, and abbreviate \(\gamma_{ij}=A_{ij}c_{ij}\). Then
\[
\tau_{\mathrm G}=\frac1N\sum_i\left(b_i+\sum_{j\ne i}\gamma_{ij}\right).
\]
Under fair cluster assignment, \(\mathbb E_Z(2Z_i-1)=0\). Also,
\[
2\mathbb E_Z\{(2Z_i-1)Z_j\}
=\begin{cases}
1,&c(j)=c(i),\\
0,&c(j)\ne c(i).
\end{cases}
\]
For a same-cluster unit, \(Z_j=Z_i\); for a different-cluster unit, the two fair assignments are independent. Substituting into the estimator gives
\[
\mathbb E_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathcal C})-\tau_{\mathrm G}
=-\frac1N\sum_i\sum_{j:c(j)\ne c(i)}\gamma_{ij}.
\tag{14}\]
The estimator captures within-cluster contributions because they move with own treatment. Across-cluster contributions cancel from its expected treatment-control comparison. For nonnegative spillovers it underestimates GATE by the omitted contribution. With mixed signs, cancellation can make bias smaller or reverse its direction.
Variance pushes the partition in the opposite direction. Even in the simple case \(Y_i(\mathbf z)=a_i\) with no effects, the estimator is random. Writing \(A_k=\sum_{i\in C_k}a_i\),
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathcal C})
=\frac4{N^2}\sum_{k=1}^K A_k^2.
\]
If all baseline outcomes equal a constant \(a\), this is \(4a^2N^{-2}\sum_k|C_k|^2\). Combining two clusters of sizes \(u\) and \(v\) increases the sum of squared sizes by \(2uv\), even if it eliminates a cut. A design criterion must weigh the expected importance of spillovers against this loss of independent variation. Covariate adjustment can change the variance calculation by replacing predictable baseline components with residuals.
The preceding calculations are a pedagogical special case. In the causal-clustering analysis, bounds on spillover strength and outcome magnitudes, along with local asymptotic restrictions, justify a corresponding worst-case optimization. Tuning the relative bias and variance penalty encodes how large relevant spillovers could be. Pilot evidence or subject knowledge can inform it, and sensitivity across plausible penalties is more informative than treating the choice as a purely graph-theoretic constant.
Changing to the exposure HT estimator changes the problem. Under a correct mapping, its bias is zero and the design concern becomes its joint exposure probabilities and variance. A partition that is attractive for Equation 13 need not be attractive for Equation 8. This is a concrete instance of designing an experiment and its analysis together.

title: L05: Interference
section: Advanced material: designs built around incompatible exposures
text:
Advanced material: designs built around incompatible exposures
Clustering begins by asking which units should share an assignment. Another starting point is to ask which outcomes needed for the estimand cannot be observed together. This makes the estimand itself part of the design’s combinatorial structure.
Fix two desired neighborhood configurations for each unit, indexed by \(a=0,1\), and let their potential outcomes be \(y_i(e_{ia})\). The target is \(N^{-1}\sum_i\{y_i(e_{i1})-y_i(e_{i0})\}\). For GATE these configurations are all treated and all control. For a direct effect at untreated neighbors, they differ only in the focal unit’s own assignment.
Two units conflict if some pair of their desired configurations cannot be realized by a single assignment vector. The conflict graph places an edge between such units, including a self-loop because one unit cannot receive both distinct configurations simultaneously. Kandiros, Pipis, Daskalakis, and Harshaw (2026) use this graph to construct a design matched to the contrast.
On the path \(1-2-3-4\), units 1 and 3 are not adjacent. Their closed neighborhoods nevertheless overlap at unit 2. Giving unit 1 its all-treated exposure requires \(Z_2=1\), while giving unit 3 its all-control exposure requires \(Z_2=0\). They conflict for GATE. In general, the GATE conflict graph connects vertices at graph distance at most two. For the direct-effect contrast that holds all neighbors untreated, units 1 and 3 can receive either desired configuration together: both require unit 2 to be untreated. For this contrast, only neighbors in the original graph conflict. The same physical network creates different observability constraints for different estimands.
The conflict-graph design first generates sparse requests for desired exposures, then resolves conflicting requests using a suitable priority ordering. Accepted requests force the necessary local treatment assignments. Its estimator uses the event that a request is accepted, not every accidental occurrence of the same exposure. If \(B_{ia}\) is that recorded event and \(q_{ia}=\mathbb P_Z(B_{ia})>0\), the form is
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{CG}}
=\frac1N\sum_i
\left\{\frac{\mathbf 1\{B_{i1}\}Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{q_{i1}}
-\frac{\mathbf 1\{B_{i0}\}Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{q_{i0}}\right\}.
\]
Accepted request \(B_{ia}\) guarantees the desired outcome, so the same HT cancellation proves unbiasedness. Restricting the counted events makes their dependence more tractable. Under bounded average squared target outcomes, the paper obtains a variance bound of order \(\lambda(H)/N\), where \(\lambda(H)\) is the largest eigenvalue of the conflict graph’s adjacency matrix, including its self-loops. This guarantee belongs to the proposed design and modified estimator together; arbitrary prioritization or the ordinary exposure HT estimator does not inherit it automatically.
For intuition about the rate, a bounded-size set of conflicts around each unit allows \(\lambda(H)\) to remain bounded and hence permits a \(1/N\) variance bound. A complete conflict graph has \(\lambda(H)=N\), so this bound no longer tends to zero. Merely increasing the number of outcomes does not create independent counterfactual comparisons when all desired exposures compete with one another.

title: L05: Interference
text:
Returning to the deployment question
Interference changes the relationship between what is assigned, what is observed, and what is wanted. The two-user science table already contained the essential issue: a person observed in a mixed assignment need not reveal their outcome under universal treatment or universal control.
An exposure assumption states when a local assignment reveals a global counterfactual. Exposure probabilities then turn this statement into an estimator, and joint probabilities govern its uncertainty. Tests can probe aspects of the assumption by designing conditional comparisons with imputable outcomes. Finally, experimental designs can make informative exposures more common, reduce the bias of a simpler estimator, or coordinate otherwise incompatible comparisons. Those are distinct statistical objectives, even when all three lead us to use a graph.
For a new application, the order of reasoning is therefore consequential: describe the mechanism and the deployment decision; state the target contrast; decide which restrictions on the science table are defensible; and choose an estimator and design that exploit those restrictions. L06 continues with restrictions on the form of the response function, where mixed assignments may be informative even without exact exposure equivalence.

title: L05: Interference
text:
Further reading
Hudgens and Halloran (2008) develop direct, indirect, total, and overall effects under partial interference, emphasizing that an allocation policy is itself an intervention. Aronow and Samii (2017) provide the design-exposure-estimand framework and the associated issues in variance estimation.
Athey, Eckles, and Imbens (2018), Saveski et al. (2017), and Han et al. (2023) give complementary routes to testing. Reading them together clarifies the distinction between sharpening a null by conditioning and changing the experiment to make its implications easier to detect.
Ugander et al. (2013) and Ugander and Yin (2023) develop fixed and randomized graph cluster designs. Eckles, Karrer, and Ugander (2017) analyze design and estimation as tools for reducing interference bias under response structures that need not satisfy a simple local exposure model. Karrer et al. (2021) discuss the practical interplay of clustering, regression adjustment, and experimentation at scale.
Viviano et al. (2026) and Kandiros et al. (2026) illustrate two different ways to turn a causal objective into a design problem: optimize a bias-variance criterion for a specified estimator, or coordinate estimand-specific observability constraints. Their guarantees should be compared with their estimator and response assumptions kept in view.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
text:
Learning about a rollout before everyone is treated
Download: Lecture PDF
Suppose a platform is testing a feature that makes it easier for users to send messages. A user’s activity may increase because they receive the feature, because their friends receive it, or because a particular combination of friends receives it. The policy question concerns a full rollout: how would average activity change if everyone received the feature? The experiment, however, treats only a random subset of users.
L05 approached this problem by describing which assignments give a unit the same outcome as the all-treated or all-control assignment. Under neighborhood interference, observing every member of a unit’s neighborhood in treatment provides its all-treated outcome. With independent treatment probability \(p\), this happens with probability \(p^{d_i}\), where \(d_i\) is the number of units in that neighborhood. These observations can be scarce even when each unit has a reasonable chance of treatment.
There is another source of information. If each friend’s contribution is additive, a neighborhood containing a mixture of treated and untreated users still reveals something about the full rollout. We need not wait until all friends receive treatment simultaneously to learn their combined contribution. If interactions occur only among pairs of friends, we need information about pairs, but not an unrestricted description of every possible neighborhood assignment.
This lecture develops that idea through the low-order outcome framework of Cortez-Rodriguez, Eichhorn, and Yu (2023). Its central move is to restrict how many treatment indicators can interact in an outcome. That restriction makes a global treatment effect a linear function of a manageable collection of coefficients. The assignment design then supplies the equations needed to estimate that linear function.
The reasoning remains design-based. The network, potential outcomes, and coefficients are fixed. Treatment assignment is random. A structural model is used to restrict the fixed potential-outcome schedule; it does not introduce random regression errors or a population of interchangeable units.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
section: A model of interactions, rather than a model of identical units
text:
A model of interactions, rather than a model of identical units

Setup and target
There are \(N\) experimental units. Write \(\mathbf z=(z_1,\ldots,z_N)\in\{0,1\}^N\) for a possible assignment and \(\mathbf Z\) for the random assignment. Unit \(i\) has potential outcome \(Y_i(\mathbf z)\) and observed outcome \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_i(\mathbf Z)\).
Let \(\mathcal N_i\) be the known set of units whose assignments can affect unit \(i\)’s outcome, including \(i\) itself. We call it a closed interference neighborhood and set \(d_i=|\mathcal N_i|\). For a directed network, membership \(j\in\mathcal N_i\) means that \(j\) can influence \(i\); the reverse need not hold. Neighborhood interference means that assignments outside \(\mathcal N_i\) do not affect \(Y_i\). A neighborhood may be a conservative superset of the actual influencing units. Missing an influencing unit is a different matter: that can invalidate the model.
The target is the global average treatment effect (GATE), also called the total treatment effect (TTE):
\[
\tau_{\mathrm G}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N
\{Y_i(\mathbf 1_N)-Y_i(\mathbf 0_N)\}.
\tag{1}\]
Here \(\mathbf 1_N\) and \(\mathbf 0_N\) assign everyone to treatment and control, respectively. This effect combines direct and spillover effects. It does not hold neighbors’ treatments fixed while changing only a unit’s own treatment.
Initially, assignments are independent, with \(Z_j\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_j)\) and known \(0<\pi_j<1\). We use \(\mathbb E_Z\) and \(\operatorname{Var}_Z\) for expectation and variance under this design, keeping the entire potential-outcome schedule fixed. Common-probability assignment is the special case \(\pi_j=p\).


Every binary response surface has a polynomial representation
For a two-person neighborhood \(\mathcal N_i=\{j,k\}\), where one of \(j,k\) is \(i\) itself, the outcome has four possible values. They can always be written as
\[
Y_i(z_j,z_k)
=c_{i,\varnothing}+c_{i,\{j\}}z_j
+c_{i,\{k\}}z_k+c_{i,\{j,k\}}z_jz_k.
\tag{2}\]
The intercept is the outcome when neither person is treated. The first-order coefficient \(c_{i,\{j\}}\) is the effect of treating \(j\) when \(k\) is untreated. The pair coefficient is the additional effect of treating both people beyond the sum of their effects when treated separately. Explicitly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{i,\varnothing}&=Y_i(0,0),\\
c_{i,\{j\}}&=Y_i(1,0)-Y_i(0,0),\\
c_{i,\{k\}}&=Y_i(0,1)-Y_i(0,0),\\
c_{i,\{j,k\}}&=Y_i(1,1)-Y_i(1,0)-Y_i(0,1)+Y_i(0,0).
\end{aligned}
\]
The interaction coefficient is a difference in the effect of \(j\) between the two treatment states of \(k\). It can be positive, negative, or zero. Thus a polynomial here is not an approximation to a smooth curve on a continuous domain. With binary inputs, it is an exact way to organize the entries of the science table.
More generally, every function on a binary neighborhood has a unique multilinear representation
\[
Y_i(\mathbf z)
=\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal N_i}c_{i,S}\prod_{j\in S}z_j.
\tag{3}\]
The product over the empty set is defined to equal one. Multilinear means that no indicator appears with a power greater than one: for binary treatment, \(z_j^2=z_j\), so higher powers add no information. There are \(2^{d_i}\) coefficients, matching the number of possible local assignments. The representation itself therefore imposes no restriction beyond neighborhood interference.
To see uniqueness, evaluate the function at the assignment treating exactly the members of some subset \(T\subseteq\mathcal N_i\). Its value is \(\sum_{S\subseteq T}c_{i,S}\). Starting with \(T=\varnothing\), then the singletons, pairs, and successively larger sets, each new equation identifies one new coefficient after subtracting the coefficients already determined.


Low order is the substantive restriction
The order-\(\beta\) model imposes
\[
c_{i,S}=0\quad\text{whenever }|S|>\beta.
\tag{4}\]
Define \(\mathcal S_i^\beta=\{S\subseteq\mathcal N_i:|S|\leq\beta\}\), including the empty set. The model becomes
\[
Y_i(\mathbf z)
=\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_i^\beta}c_{i,S}\prod_{j\in S}z_j.
\tag{5}\]
For \(\beta=1\), all influences are additive. A unit can have many influencing neighbors, and their effects can all differ. For \(\beta=2\), any pair of assignments can interact, but the contribution of that pair cannot depend on a third assignment. Neither specification requires common coefficients across units. The effect of \(j\) on \(i\) may differ from its effect on \(k\), and direct effects may differ throughout the network.
Low order consequently differs from low degree in the network. A user with hundreds of friends can satisfy an additive model. Conversely, an outcome that changes only when all three members of a small neighborhood receive treatment requires a third-order term. It also differs from assuming that only the fraction of treated neighbors matters: the polynomial allows different friends to matter differently.
The number of retained coefficients for unit \(i\) is \(K_i=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\beta,d_i)}\binom{d_i}{r}\). For fixed small \(\beta\), this grows polynomially with neighborhood size, rather than as \(2^{d_i}\). But choosing a small order is a scientific assumption, not merely a way to reduce computation. A threshold or saturation response need not have small degree just because its verbal description is simple.


The global effect is a sum of coefficients
At the all-treated assignment, every product in Equation 5 equals one. At the all-control assignment, only the empty-set term remains. Therefore,
\[
Y_i(\mathbf 1_N)-Y_i(\mathbf 0_N)
=\sum_{\substack{S\in\mathcal S_i^\beta\\S\ne\varnothing}}c_{i,S},
\qquad
\tau_{\mathrm G}=\frac1N\sum_i\sum_{\substack{S\in\mathcal S_i^\beta\\S\ne\varnothing}}c_{i,S}.
\tag{6}\]
The intercept cancels, but every nonempty interaction enters the global contrast. We have converted the causal target into a linear function of the coefficients. We next ask whether the experiment can estimate that function without learning each response surface accurately.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
text:
Start with additive spillovers

Randomization isolates a neighbor’s contribution
Under \(\beta=1\), write the response as
\[
Y_i(\mathbf Z)=c_{i,\varnothing}
+\sum_{k\in\mathcal N_i}c_{i,\{k\}}Z_k.
\]
To learn the contribution of a particular neighbor \(j\), multiply the observed outcome by the centered treatment indicator \(Z_j-\pi_j\). Independence makes this indicator uncorrelated with the intercept and with every other neighbor’s assignment. The one surviving term is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_Z[Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}(Z_j-\pi_j)]
&=c_{i,\varnothing}\mathbb E_Z[Z_j-\pi_j]
+\sum_{k\in\mathcal N_i}c_{i,\{k\}}
  \mathbb E_Z[Z_k(Z_j-\pi_j)]\\
&=c_{i,\{j\}}\pi_j(1-\pi_j).
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]
Dividing by the treatment variance gives an unbiased estimator of \(c_{i,\{j\}}\). Summing these estimates over \(j\) and then averaging over outcome units yields
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{SNIPE}(1)}
=\frac1N\sum_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}
\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}\frac{Z_j-\pi_j}{\pi_j(1-\pi_j)}.
\tag{8}\]
SNIPE stands for Structured Neighborhood Interference Polynomial Estimator (Cortez-Rodriguez, Eichhorn, and Yu 2023). Each outcome receives a weight determined by the assignments of all units that can influence it. For additive interference, the weight accumulates the evidence supplied by each neighbor’s randomized assignment.
This expression has the familiar Horvitz–Thompson estimator as a special case. If \(\mathcal N_i=\{i\}\), then
\[
\frac{Z_i-\pi_i}{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)}
=\frac{Z_i}{\pi_i}-\frac{1-Z_i}{1-\pi_i}.
\]
Under interference, observing \(Y_i\) gives information about effects associated with several assignments, not just \(Z_i\). The extra terms use that information under the additive restriction.


An explicit four-assignment calculation
Consider one outcome with neighborhood \(\{1,2\}\) and response \(Y_i(z_1,z_2)=10+2z_1+3z_2\). The global contrast for this unit is \(5\). Under independent fair coins, each of the four assignments occurs with probability \(1/4\). Let \(\ell_i\) denote the inner sum of weights in Equation 8. The contribution from this outcome is \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\ell_i\).

\(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\)
\(\ell_i=4(Z_1-1/2)+4(Z_2-1/2)\)

The average of the last column is \(5\). A single contribution can nevertheless be far from \(5\). Unbiasedness does not mean that one observed outcome estimates all of its coefficients precisely. Precision, if available, comes from averaging contributions across many units while controlling their dependence.
The intercept of 10 contributes random noise although it cancels from the target. Subtracting a known baseline would leave the expectation unchanged and could improve precision. We return to this observation when introducing covariate adjustment.
With two neighbors and fair coins, the mixed assignments happen to receive zero weight. This cancellation is special. With three neighbors and fair coins, the weight is \(4\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}Z_j-6\), which equals \(-2\) or \(2\) for mixed assignments containing one or two treated units. Those assignments directly contribute to the estimator.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
section: From coefficient estimation to the pseudoinverse
text:
From coefficient estimation to the pseudoinverse

The known design replaces a missing regression sample
The additive calculation used independence to isolate one coefficient. A matrix formulation will handle interactions and more general designs with the same underlying logic.
Choose an ordering of \(\mathcal S_i^\beta\), putting the empty set first. Let \(\mathbf v_i(\mathbf z)\) be the \(K_i\)-dimensional column vector whose entry indexed by \(S\) is \(\prod_{j\in S}z_j\). Let \(\mathbf c_i\) collect the coefficients in the same order. For example, with two neighbors and \(\beta=2\),
\[
\mathbf v_i(\mathbf z)=(1,z_1,z_2,z_1z_2)^\top,
\qquad
Y_i(\mathbf z)=\mathbf v_i(\mathbf z)^\top\mathbf c_i.
\]
The vector \(\mathbf a_i=\mathbf v_i(\mathbf 1_N)-\mathbf v_i(\mathbf 0_N)\) has first entry zero and all remaining entries one. It specifies the desired coefficient sum: the unit’s global contrast is \(\mathbf a_i^\top\mathbf c_i\).
Now imagine, only as a thought experiment, repeating the assignment many times for the same unit with its response function unchanged. With enough repeated assignments, ordinary least squares would regress the repeated outcomes on the corresponding feature vectors. The population normal equations would be
\[
\underbrace{\mathbb E_Z[
\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)^\top]}_{\mathbf M_i}
\mathbf c_i
=\mathbb E_Z[\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}].
\tag{9}\]
The \(K_i\times K_i\) matrix \(\mathbf M_i\) is the design moment matrix. Its entries depend on assignment probabilities, not unknown outcome coefficients. For Bernoulli assignment,
\[
(\mathbf M_i)_{S,T}
=\mathbb E_Z\left[\prod_{j\in S\cup T}Z_j\right]
=\prod_{j\in S\cup T}\pi_j.
\tag{10}\]
The union appears because an indicator present in both products still equals itself when squared. The first entry, indexed by two empty sets, equals one.
In the actual experiment we have one outcome per unit, not a sample of repeated outcomes for each unit. We therefore cannot run a separate ordinary regression and identify all of its coefficients from that one row. Nor can we silently pool units: their coefficient vectors are allowed to differ.
What we can do is use the known left-hand matrix in Equation 9 and an unbiased, one-observation estimate of its right-hand side. When \(\mathbf M_i\) is invertible,
\[
\widehat{\mathbf c}_i
=\mathbf M_i^{-1}\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}},
\qquad
\mathbb E_Z[\widehat{\mathbf c}_i]=\mathbf c_i.
\tag{11}\]
The apparent abundance of unbiased coefficient estimates is not an abundance of information in one realized assignment. All entries of \(\widehat{\mathbf c}_i\) use the same outcome and can be very noisy and strongly dependent. Their expectations recover the coefficients across assignments.


What singularity means
Independent Bernoulli assignment with every probability strictly between zero and one gives positive probability to every local assignment. The distinct multilinear features are linearly independent on that support, so \(\mathbf M_i\) is positive definite. Other designs can make it singular. For example, always assigning two neighbors together makes their two treatment indicators identical in every experiment.
The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, written \(\mathbf M_i^\dagger\), inverts the nonzero eigenvalues of this symmetric matrix and leaves its zero eigenvalues at zero. The associated estimator is
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{PI}}
=\frac1N\sum_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\ell_i(\mathbf Z),
\qquad
\ell_i(\mathbf Z)
=\mathbf a_i^\top\mathbf M_i^\dagger\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z).
\tag{12}\]
PI denotes pseudoinverse. This is the pseudoinverse of an expectation under the design, not the pseudoinverse of the single realized outer product \(\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)^\top\).

Proposition 1 (When the pseudoinverse estimates the desired contrast) Suppose the order-\(\beta\) response model holds. If \(\mathbf a_i\) lies in the column space of \(\mathbf M_i\) for every \(i\), then \(\mathbb E_Z[\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{PI}}]=\tau_{\mathrm G}\). Because \(\mathbf M_i\) is symmetric, its column and row spaces coincide.


Proof. For each unit, substitute \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)^\top\mathbf c_i\) to obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_Z[Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\ell_i(\mathbf Z)]
&=\mathbf a_i^\top\mathbf M_i^\dagger
\mathbb E_Z[\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)^\top]
\mathbf c_i\\
&=\mathbf a_i^\top\mathbf M_i^\dagger\mathbf M_i\mathbf c_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
The matrix \(\mathbf P_i=\mathbf M_i^\dagger\mathbf M_i\) is the orthogonal projection onto the column space of \(\mathbf M_i\). The stated condition gives \(\mathbf a_i^\top\mathbf P_i=\mathbf a_i^\top\), so the expectation is \(\mathbf a_i^\top\mathbf c_i\). Average these equalities over units.

Singularity can thus prevent estimation of individual coefficients without preventing estimation of their sum. If two neighbors always move together, their separate additive effects cannot be distinguished, but their combined effect may remain estimable. The target contrast, not the full coefficient vector, determines the required support condition.
The condition is also necessary for unbiased estimation of every possible coefficient vector in this unrestricted unit-specific model. If it fails, there is a vector \(\mathbf b_i\) in the null space of \(\mathbf M_i\) for which \(\mathbf a_i^\top\mathbf b_i\ne0\). Since
\[
0=\mathbf b_i^\top\mathbf M_i\mathbf b_i
=\mathbb E_Z[(\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)^\top\mathbf b_i)^2],
\]
adding \(\mathbf b_i\) to the coefficients changes no outcome on the design’s support. It does change the desired global contrast. The experiment cannot distinguish these two response schedules. Applying a pseudoinverse does not resolve this identification failure; it selects the projection that is visible under the design.


The geometry behind the weights
The estimation problem can also be expressed without estimating coefficients. We want a random weight \(w_i(\mathbf Z)\) that reproduces the global contrast for every allowed polynomial response. That requires the coordinatewise moment equations
\[
\mathbb E_Z[w_i(\mathbf Z)\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)]
=\mathbf a_i.
\tag{13}\]
The first equation says the weight has mean zero, so a constant outcome makes no contribution in expectation. Every other equation says that a permitted treatment product receives the correct coefficient of one in the target.
When the estimability condition holds, these equations are feasible. Among weights satisfying them, \(\ell_i\) in Equation 12 has minimum \(\mathbb E_Z[w_i^2]\). Indeed, if \(w_i=\ell_i+r_i\), the moment equations give \(\mathbb E_Z[r_i\mathbf v_i]=0\). Since \(\ell_i\) is a linear combination of these features, \(\mathbb E_Z[r_i\ell_i]=0\), and
\[
\mathbb E_Z[w_i^2]
=\mathbb E_Z[\ell_i^2]+\mathbb E_Z[r_i^2].
\]
This is a least-squares projection argument: the additional component of a weight orthogonal to the allowed response features cannot help reproduce their contrast. Minimum squared weight is useful for controlling noise, but it is not a universal minimum-variance claim for the whole estimator. Outcomes differ across assignments, and contributions from different units can covary.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
text:
Higher-order interactions under independent assignment

Centering provides an orthogonal basis
The raw monomial matrix can be large. Independent assignment gives a more transparent route to the same estimator. For a subset \(S\) of the neighborhood, define the centered product
\[
u_S(\mathbf Z)=\prod_{j\in S}(Z_j-\pi_j),
\qquad u_\varnothing(\mathbf Z)=1.
\]
If \(S\ne T\), some indicator occurs in exactly one of the products. Its mean-zero factor and independence imply \(\mathbb E_Z[u_Su_T]=0\). Moreover, \(\mathbb E_Z[u_S^2]=\prod_{j\in S}\pi_j(1-\pi_j)\). These centered products span the same order-\(\beta\) polynomial space as the raw products. Subtracting constants from the inputs changes coefficients, but not the maximum degree.
We can therefore write \(Y_i(\mathbf z)=\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_i^\beta}b_{i,S}u_S(\mathbf z)\), where the \(b_{i,S}\) are coefficients in this centered basis. Orthogonality gives
\[
\mathbb E_Z\left[
Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}
\frac{u_S(\mathbf Z)}{\prod_{j\in S}\pi_j(1-\pi_j)}
\right]=b_{i,S}.
\]
The global contrast of the basis function \(u_S\) is
\[
\Delta_S=u_S(\mathbf 1_N)-u_S(\mathbf 0_N)
=\prod_{j\in S}(1-\pi_j)-\prod_{j\in S}(-\pi_j).
\]
For the empty set this difference is zero. Combining the unbiased estimates of the centered coefficients with their global contrasts gives
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{SNIPE}(\beta)}
=\frac1N\sum_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}
\sum_{\substack{S\in\mathcal S_i^\beta\\S\ne\varnothing}}
\Delta_S\prod_{j\in S}
\frac{Z_j-\pi_j}{\pi_j(1-\pi_j)}.
\tag{14}\]
This explicit formula equals Equation 12 under independent Bernoulli assignment. The centered basis diagonalizes the design inner product, doing the work that matrix inversion performs in the raw basis.


A pair interaction and a revealing cancellation
Consider again a two-person neighborhood, now with \(Y_i(z_1,z_2)=10+2z_1+3z_2+4z_1z_2\). Its global contrast is \(9\). Take common treatment probability \(p=1/4\) and define \(q_j=(Z_j-p)/\{p(1-p)\}\). Each singleton has \(\Delta_{\{j\}}=1\), while \(\Delta_{\{1,2\}}=(1-p)^2-p^2=1-2p=1/2\). The order-two weight is
\[
\ell_i=q_1+q_2+\tfrac12q_1q_2.
\]
The first two terms alone recover the additive contribution \(5\) plus \(2p\cdot4=2\) from the pair interaction. To check the latter statement, \(\mathbb E_Z[Z_1Z_2q_1]=p\) and \(\mathbb E_Z[Z_1Z_2q_2]=p\). The pair term supplies the missing amount: \(\mathbb E_Z[Z_1Z_2q_1q_2]=1\), so its contribution is \((1/2)\cdot4=2\). The expectation of the full contribution is therefore \(5+2+2=9\).
This calculation also explains why the additive estimator is generally biased when pair interactions are present. It estimates only the part of the pair effect that appears when the other member is treated at the experiment’s assignment probability. The full rollout requires that other member to be treated with certainty.
There is an instructive exception. At \(p=1/2\), the pair contrast \(\Delta_{\{1,2\}}\) is zero, so the order-two and order-one SNIPE weights coincide. Pair effects still enter the GATE. They are already captured through the first-order centered coefficients: changing from raw to centered products moves part of a raw pair term into the linear terms. For the example above, the additive weight at \(p=1/2\) recovers \(5+2p\cdot4=9\).
This cancellation does not make arbitrary high-order interactions harmless. For a raw triple term \(\gamma z_1z_2z_3\), the order-one weight at common probability \(p\) has expectation \(3p^2\gamma\), rather than \(\gamma\). At \(p=1/2\) it recovers only \(3\gamma/4\). Correctness depends jointly on the target, the response model, and the design.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
section: Precision requires information about shared assignments
text:
Precision requires information about shared assignments

Interaction order controls a local difficulty
The centered representation makes the squared size of a unit’s weight explicit:
\[
\mathbb E_Z[\ell_i^2]
=\sum_{\substack{S\in\mathcal S_i^\beta\\S\ne\varnothing}}
\frac{\Delta_S^2}{\prod_{j\in S}\pi_j(1-\pi_j)}.
\tag{15}\]
Products of small treatment probabilities still matter. However, the largest product now involves at most \(\beta\) units, rather than the entire neighborhood. For fixed \(\beta\) and probabilities bounded away from zero and one, the number of terms grows polynomially with \(d_i\). This is the mechanism by which low order can improve precision relative to requiring full neighborhood exposure. It does not guarantee small variance for every network or every outcome schedule.
For additive interference with common \(p\), the formula simplifies to \(\mathbb E_Z[\ell_i^2]=d_i/\{p(1-p)\}\). Each extra influencing assignment adds to the random fluctuation of the weight. A high-degree outcome can be informative about many treatment contributions, but that information is not costless.


Shared neighbors generate covariance
Let \(T_i=Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\ell_i(\mathbf Z)\) be unit \(i\)’s contribution. The exact variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{PI}})
=\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,k}\operatorname{Cov}_Z(T_i,T_k).
\tag{16}\]
Under independent unit assignment and neighborhood interference, \(T_i\) and \(T_k\) are independent when \(\mathcal N_i\cap\mathcal N_k=\varnothing\). When their neighborhoods overlap, one treatment coin can affect both weighted outcomes. The number of units is therefore not the number of independent pieces of information.
A simple bound exposes this distinction. Suppose \(|Y_i(\mathbf z)|\leq B\) for all units and assignments, let \(\mathbb E_Z[\ell_i^2]\leq A\), and suppose each neighborhood overlaps with at most \(D\) neighborhoods, counting itself. By Cauchy–Schwarz, \(|\operatorname{Cov}_Z(T_i,T_k)|\leq B^2A\). There are at most \(ND\) potentially nonzero covariance terms, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{PI}})
\leq\frac{B^2AD}{N}.
\tag{17}\]
This deliberately elementary bound separates three difficulties: outcome magnitude, the size of the weights, and dependence across contributions. It also shows why bounding neighborhood size alone is insufficient in a directed network. A single influential unit may appear in many small neighborhoods, creating widespread dependence.
Cortez-Rodriguez, Eichhorn, and Yu (2023) give sharper variance bounds and asymptotic normality results under their network and outcome regularity conditions. Such results require a sequence of experiments in which dependence and influential contributions remain controlled. Exact unbiasedness by itself supplies neither a central limit theorem nor a reliable standard error.


Inference is a further problem
An empirical variance treating the \(T_i\) as independent drops the covariance terms in Equation 16. A usual regression standard error does not recover those terms either. The relevant dependence comes from shared assignments, and uncertainty calculations must reflect it.
Even with a known design, exact variance estimation is difficult. The variance contains products of unknown potential-outcome coefficients, while each unit reveals only one outcome. Unbiased estimation of each coefficient does not imply that multiplying two estimated coefficients gives an unbiased estimate of their product. Conservative bounds and dependence-aware asymptotic variance estimators address different parts of this difficulty. A normal approximation should be paired with a justified variance procedure and the assumptions under which the approximation is valid.
For a small network, exact enumeration is useful for checking an implementation under a specified response schedule. It is a simulation exercise: the missing potential outcomes are supplied by the analyst. It does not turn the variance under the real, unknown schedule into an observed quantity.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
section: Changing the design while retaining the model
text:
Changing the design while retaining the model
The moment equations did not require independent treatment assignment. What changes under a different design is \(\mathbf M_i\), its column space, and the covariance between contributions. Eichhorn, Khan, Ugander, and Yu (2026) develop this general-design perspective, with particular attention to clustered experiments.
If two additive neighbors always receive the same cluster assignment \(W\), then
\[
Y_i=c_{i,\varnothing}+(c_{i,\{1\}}+c_{i,\{2\}})W.
\]
The separate effects are indistinguishable, but the sum is the global contrast and is identified when \(0<\mathbb P_Z(W=1)<1\). The moment matrix based on \((1,Z_1,Z_2)\) is singular; its null direction changes the two coefficients by opposite amounts and leaves their sum unchanged. This is exactly the favorable case in Proposition 1.
More generally, under independent Bernoulli assignment of clusters, every configuration of the clusters touching a neighborhood has positive probability. If a polynomial vanishes on this support, it vanishes at both the all-treated and all-control cluster assignments, so its global contrast is zero. The desired contrast is therefore estimable even when the original unit-level coefficient vector is not.
Complete randomization of a fixed number of clusters can behave differently. For an extreme example, take a two-unit neighborhood and always treat exactly one of its members. The two additive schedules \(Y_i(\mathbf z)=0\) and \(Y_i(\mathbf z)=z_1+z_2-1\) agree at both supported assignments. Their all-treated-minus-all-control contrasts are \(0\) and \(2\). No estimator can distinguish them under this design. A restriction on total treatment count can remove precisely the variation needed to learn a global rollout effect.
Clustering also changes precision. It can reduce the number of independently varying treatment components relevant to an outcome, while correlating the weighted outcomes of more units. The cited work combines these effects in design-specific bounds and uses the bounds to compare candidate clusterings. The lesson is to choose the design and analysis together: a low-order model does not eliminate the reasons to cluster, and clustering does not eliminate the value of outcome structure.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
section: Covariate adjustment should target the estimator’s variance
text:
Covariate adjustment should target the estimator’s variance
The additive example showed that a large baseline outcome can create noise without changing the GATE. Suppose \(X_i\) is a fixed vector of pretreatment covariates predictive of that baseline. Since the first coordinate of Equation 13 gives \(\mathbb E_Z[\ell_i]=0\), any fixed coefficient vector \(\theta\) yields the adjusted estimator
\[
\widehat\tau(\theta)
=\frac1N\sum_i\ell_i(\mathbf Z)
\{Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-X_i^\top\theta\}.
\tag{18}\]
Its expectation is still \(\tau_{\mathrm G}\) whenever the original estimator is unbiased. The adjustment subtracts a random quantity with known mean zero. No correct linear model relating outcomes to \(X_i\) is required for this fixed-\(\theta\) statement.
To see how to choose \(\theta\), define the random covariate vector \(\mathbf H=N^{-1}\sum_i\ell_iX_i\), with \(\mathbb E_Z[\mathbf H]=0\). Then \(\widehat\tau(\theta)=\widehat\tau(0)-\theta^\top\mathbf H\) and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}_Z\{\widehat\tau(\theta)\}
=\operatorname{Var}_Z\{\widehat\tau(0)\}
-2\theta^\top\operatorname{Cov}_Z\{\mathbf H,\widehat\tau(0)\}
+\theta^\top\operatorname{Var}_Z(\mathbf H)\theta.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}\]
If \(\operatorname{Var}_Z(\mathbf H)\) is invertible, the oracle choice is its inverse times \(\operatorname{Cov}_Z\{\mathbf H,\widehat\tau(0)\}\). This choice minimizes the variance of the final effect estimator. Ordinary regression of observed outcomes on covariates solves a different objective, and can neglect cross-unit covariance induced by interference.
Wang and Li (2026) make this difference central. Their variance-improvement-maximized (VIM) procedure estimates the change in variance from adjusting and chooses coefficients to maximize that improvement. A useful cancellation makes this feasible: the variance of the unadjusted estimator contains quadratic terms in unknown response coefficients, but those terms cancel when subtracting the adjusted variance. The remaining improvement can be estimated using the coefficient-estimation machinery already developed.
Their no-harm guarantee concerns the asymptotic variance of this particular procedure under the stated sparsity, moment, and coefficient-estimation conditions. It is not a guarantee for arbitrary regression adjustment or for every realized sample. Fixed coefficients preserve exact unbiasedness; fitting \(\widehat\theta\) using the same experimental outcomes introduces additional randomness and requires an asymptotic argument. The paper also develops an asymptotically conservative variance estimator for inference.
In practice, choose covariates before examining treatment effects, use the dependence-aware adjustment procedure rather than substituting a familiar regression by analogy, and inspect whether the network conditions supporting its approximation are plausible. Randomly splitting outcome units does not automatically produce independent training and evaluation data, because their outcomes can depend on the same treatment coins.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
text:
Other structural information: monotone interference

Restricting directions instead of interaction order
An intervention may plausibly benefit from wider adoption without producing an additive response. A messaging feature might become useful only when a critical mass of friends uses it. A vaccination may become more protective as more neighbors are vaccinated. In such settings, the sign of a spillover can be more defensible than a low-order polynomial model.
One possible restriction is coordinatewise monotonicity: if \(\mathbf z\leq\mathbf z'\) in every coordinate, then \(Y_i(\mathbf z)\leq Y_i(\mathbf z')\). For spillovers alone, one might impose this ordering only while holding \(z_i\) fixed. The sign must match the outcome: beneficial vaccination could make disease incidence nonincreasing. These are substantive restrictions on potential outcomes, not consequences of randomization.
Monotonicity and low order are distinct. The function \(\prod_{j\in\mathcal N_i}z_j\) is monotone and can have arbitrarily high order. An additive model with one positive and one negative coefficient is low order but not coordinatewise nondecreasing. Nor does monotonicity force every raw polynomial coefficient to be nonnegative: the function \(z_1+z_2-z_1z_2\), representing whether at least one person is treated, is monotone and has a negative pair coefficient.


What monotonicity can provide
For a simple illustration, define the marginal-treatment estimator
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{marg}}
=\frac1N\sum_i\left\{
\frac{Z_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\pi_i}
-\frac{(1-Z_i)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{1-\pi_i}\right\}.
\]
Its expectation compares the outcome conditional on own treatment to that conditional on own control. Under full coordinatewise nondecreasing outcomes, every outcome observed when \(Z_i=1\) is at most \(Y_i(\mathbf 1_N)\), and every outcome observed when \(Z_i=0\) is at least \(Y_i(\mathbf 0_N)\). Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E_Z[\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{marg}}]\leq\tau_{\mathrm G}.
\tag{20}\]
This is a directional bias statement. It is neither a point-identification result for \(\tau_{\mathrm G}\) nor a claim that a realized estimate is a lower confidence bound. Establishing uncertainty around a bound needs further inference.
Several papers use structural inequalities for different purposes:

Choi (2017) develops confidence intervals for attributable effects, comparing outcomes under the realized assignment with outcomes under no treatment. The restrictions resemble nonnegative treatment effects and do not require partial interference. That attributable-effect target differs from the all-treated-versus-all-control GATE.
Eckles, Karrer, and Ugander (2017) use monotonicity and related conditions to study bias reduction through correlated assignment and exposure-based analysis, allowing potentially global interference. Their conditions explain when moving experimental exposure closer to a global policy comparison reduces bias; they do not make every clustering universally preferable.
Pouget-Abadie and colleagues (2018) study comparing clustered designs when the corresponding estimators are biased in a common direction. If both expected estimates lie below the target, the larger expected estimate is closer to it. Their experiment-of-experiments design addresses how to compare clusterings experimentally. Here the relevant monotonicity is a property of bias across a family of designs, which should not be conflated with one generic unit-level inequality.
Huang, Li, and Toulis (2025) develop finite-sample-valid randomization tests for monotone spillover contrasts using appropriate conditioning and network constructions. An inequality null does not reveal every missing potential outcome as a sharp null does; valid testing needs that additional construction. Such tests concern directional hypotheses, not unrestricted estimation of the GATE.

Submodularity is another possible restriction. Viewing an outcome as a function of the treated set, it says that the incremental effect of adding a given treated unit is no larger when the already-treated set is larger. It formalizes diminishing returns. It can coexist with monotonicity but is not implied by it, and it does not impose low polynomial order. The appropriate structure depends on the mechanism one is prepared to defend.
The central lesson of the lecture is that a partially treated network can inform a global rollout through several different kinds of structure. Low order turns the rollout contrast into a linear coefficient functional, and randomization supplies unbiased estimating equations for that functional. Monotonicity instead supplies inequalities. In either case, the experiment’s design determines what variation is available, and the structural assumption determines what that variation can tell us about unobserved assignments.
