title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
section: Advanced material: model error and the cost of extrapolation
text:
Advanced material: model error and the cost of extrapolation

An exact bias decomposition
Suppose a chosen order-\(\beta\) model leaves a remainder:
\[
Y_i(\mathbf z)=\mathbf v_i(\mathbf z)^\top\mathbf c_i+R_i(\mathbf z).
\]
Assume the contrast is estimable for the retained polynomial space. The polynomial part remains unbiased, so the bias of the estimator for the actual GATE is exactly
\[
\mathbb E_Z[\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{PI}}]-\tau_{\mathrm G}
=\frac1N\sum_i\left[
\mathbb E_Z\{\ell_i(\mathbf Z)R_i(\mathbf Z)\}
-\{R_i(\mathbf 1_N)-R_i(\mathbf 0_N)\}
\right].
\tag{21}\]
Two features matter: how the omitted response aligns with the estimator’s weight over the experimental distribution, and how much it contributes at the two policy endpoints. A model can fit typical experimental assignments well while misrepresenting the full rollout. With low treatment probability, a high-order interaction may rarely activate in the experiment yet contribute substantially when everyone is treated.
For example, if \(|R_i(\mathbf z)|\leq\varepsilon_i\) uniformly over all assignments, Cauchy–Schwarz yields the bound
\[
|\operatorname{Bias}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{PI}})|
\leq\frac1N\sum_i\varepsilon_i
\left\{\sqrt{\mathbb E_Z[\ell_i^2]}+2\right\}.
\]
The uniform qualification is doing work: accuracy only on assignments that occur frequently does not control the endpoint remainder. Large weights also amplify model error over the experimental distribution.
If the contrast is not estimable under the design, there is an additional polynomial bias term \(N^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf a_i^\top(\mathbf P_i-\mathbf I)\mathbf c_i\), where \(\mathbf P_i=\mathbf M_i^\dagger\mathbf M_i\) and \(\mathbf I\) is the identity matrix. This separates lack of design support from misspecifying the outcome class. Either can obstruct the target, and they call for different responses.


Choosing an order and extending the experiment
Increasing \(\beta\) includes more response schedules but can increase the number and size of weights. A defensible analysis should connect the chosen order to a mechanism, examine sensitivity to plausible higher-order effects, and consider whether the design can improve the relevant treatment variation. Selecting the order after searching for a favorable estimated effect is not covered by the fixed-model unbiasedness argument.
The downstream literature also changes what data are collected. Under a common Bernoulli treatment probability \(p\), the design mean of an order-\(\beta\) response is a univariate polynomial in \(p\):
\[
\frac1N\sum_i\mathbb E_{Z,p}[Y_i(\mathbf Z)]
=\frac1N\sum_i\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_i^\beta}c_{i,S}p^{|S|}.
\]
Its value at one minus its value at zero is the GATE. Varying treatment saturation across rollout stages can therefore replace some detailed network information with observations at several values of \(p\). But extrapolating a polynomial from a narrow range of probabilities to a full rollout can be unstable. Repeated stages also require a stable response interpretation, with time and carryover effects addressed by the design and assumptions.
Cortez-Rodriguez, Eichhorn, and Yu (2025) study a two-stage rollout that first selects a subpopulation and then rolls out treatment within it. Their analysis connects bias to cut edges and variance to clustering properties including covariate balance. Alongside clustered pseudoinverse estimation and VIM covariate adjustment, this is a concrete development beyond the original SNIPE construction: improve the information available to the estimator, rather than expecting an outcome restriction alone to solve every precision problem.

title: L06: Estimation with Structural Models
text:
Further reading
Cortez-Rodriguez, Eichhorn, and Yu (2023) are the main source for this lecture. The centered-basis derivation above is a way to see the estimator’s mechanics; the paper supplies the broader variance and asymptotic analysis. Eichhorn and colleagues (2026) extend the construction to general designs and make design selection part of the analysis. Their preprint first appeared in 2024; the cited version was revised in 2026.
For subsequent work, Wang and Li (2026) distinguish predicting outcomes well from reducing the variance of an interference estimator, while Cortez-Rodriguez and colleagues (2025) develop the rollout-design direction. These are complementary routes: use covariates, change dependence through clustering, or observe more than one treatment saturation.
The monotonicity papers cited above ask different causal questions with different inequalities. Reading them together is useful precisely because monotonicity is not one transferable assumption with one universal conclusion. Track the target, the direction of the restriction, the experimental design, and whether the result concerns bias, a bound, or a hypothesis test.

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
text:
Evaluate a rule, not just a treatment label
Download: Lecture PDF
A public-health campaign can contact a small number of people in each village and hope that information spreads. Suppose the budget permits contacting one person. One strategy chooses that person uniformly at random. Another chooses a random resident, asks them to name a friend, and contacts the friend. Both strategies deliver the same intervention to one person. They differ in which person is likely to receive it.
The policy question is about the resulting diffusion through the village: which strategy produces more adoption, at the same contact budget? Comparing outcomes of contacted and uncontacted people is not the relevant comparison. An uncontacted person who learns from a neighbor is part of the strategy’s success. The causal intervention is the rule used to choose seeds, and its outcome includes the responses of people who were not seeded.
Chin, Eckles, and Ugander (2022) study precisely this evaluation problem. Their formulation connects network experiments to policy evaluation: learning the expected outcome under a specified rule for assigning an intervention. A policy can be stochastic, meaning that it assigns probabilities to several possible interventions rather than always choosing the same one.
This perspective continues L05. There we distinguished changing a person’s own treatment from changing the surrounding treatment environment. Here we specify a distribution over those environments and ask how well that distribution performs. The known randomization law will let us evaluate more than the experimental arm labels alone.
crumbs: 9  L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
text:
Potential outcomes for whole seed sets
Consider \(M\) villages, indexed by \(g=1,\ldots,M\). Village \(g\) has a fixed pretreatment graph with vertex set \(V_g\), and \(\mathcal S_g\) is its set of allowable seed sets. For example, with a budget of \(k\) distinct contacts, \(\mathcal S_g=\{s\subseteq V_g:|s|=k\}\). Let \(Y_g(s)\) be the number of adopters in that village at a specified follow-up time if seed set \(s\) were contacted.
All of these potential outcomes and graphs are fixed in the initial design-based argument. Randomness comes from selecting the seed sets. If diffusion itself is modeled as random, an additional expectation over that process must be stated; it is not silently included in the assignment expectation below.
Arbitrary interference within a village is allowed: \(Y_g(s)\) summarizes the entire response to the selected set. Two other restrictions are important. First, one village’s seed set must not change another village’s outcome. Second, the strategy label must have no effect beyond the realized seed set. If two strategies select the same people but train them differently, their potential outcomes cannot be indexed by the set alone. The intervention would need to include the training protocol.
A policy \(p\) specifies known probabilities \(p_g(s)\) over \(\mathcal S_g\) for each village. Its finite-population value is
\[
V_M(p)=\frac1M\sum_{g=1}^M
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_g}p_g(s)Y_g(s).
\tag{1}\]
There are two averages here: first over the policy’s possible seed sets in a particular village, then over the villages. This target is the average number of adopters per village, not the average treatment effect on a seeded person. If village sizes differ, average adoption rates or a resident-weighted target would be different choices. Specify that choice through the outcome and the village weights before estimating anything.
For two fixed policies \(A\) and \(B\), write
\[
\Delta_M(A,B)=V_M(p^A)-V_M(p^B)
=\frac1M\sum_g\sum_s
\{p_g^A(s)-p_g^B(s)\}Y_g(s).
\tag{2}\]
The same potential outcome can receive positive weight, negative weight, or zero weight depending on how the strategies change its probability. Evaluating a stochastic policy is thus an average of causal interventions, not an attempt to declare each realized seed set a new experimental arm.


A four-person example
Take a star with one center \(c\) connected to three leaves \(a,b,d\). Consider one seed and a deliberately simple response: the seed adopts, and adoption then spreads to its immediate neighbors in one transmission step. It does not continue to a second step. Consequently, seeding the center produces four adopters, while seeding any leaf produces two.
Policy \(B\) chooses a uniform seed. Policy \(A\) chooses a uniform resident and then a uniform neighbor of that resident. The center is named whenever one of the three leaves is chosen first. A particular leaf is named only when the center is chosen first and then selects that leaf.

The two values are
\[
V(p^B)=\frac14(4)+\frac34(2)=\frac52,
\qquad
V(p^A)=\frac34(4)+\frac14(2)=\frac72.
\]
The policy gain is one additional adopter, averaged over the random choice of seed. This is an illustrative science table, not an empirical finding about one-hop targeting. If deterministic adoption instead continued until everyone reachable from the seed had adopted, all four seeds would produce four adopters and the policy contrast would be zero. The outcome horizon and diffusion mechanism matter as much as the graph.
For a general undirected graph without isolated vertices, let \(\mathcal A_g(u)\) be the neighbors of \(u\), excluding \(u\) itself, and let \(\deg_g(u)=|\mathcal A_g(u)|\). The one-hop probability of selecting vertex \(v\) is
\[
p_g^A(\{v\})
=\frac1{|V_g|}\sum_{u:\,v\in\mathcal A_g(u)}
\frac1{\deg_g(u)}.
\tag{3}\]
Each possible nominator supplies one route to choosing \(v\). This distribution is not generally proportional to \(v\)’s degree: being connected to a person with few friends gives a larger nomination probability than being connected to someone with many friends. Isolated vertices require an explicit protocol for failed nominations.
For several seeds, the complete sampling algorithm matters. Sampling with replacement, conditioning all nominations on being distinct, and rejecting duplicates sequentially need not yield the same distribution over sets. Inverse-probability weights must use the probability of the actual seed set under the implemented algorithm. A verbal label such as “friend targeting” does not specify those probabilities.

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
section: Evaluate a policy using the experiment we actually ran
text:
Evaluate a policy using the experiment we actually ran

The design and the target need not be the same distribution
Suppose the experiment draws \(S_g\sim q_g\) independently across villages and observes \(Y_g^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_g(S_g)\). The distribution \(q_g\) is the known experimental design; \(p_g^A\) and \(p_g^B\) are the policies we wish to evaluate. This is often called off-policy evaluation when a target policy differs from the data-generating policy.
For now assume that \(q_g(s)>0\) whenever either target policy assigns positive probability to \(s\). Define
\[
w_g^a(s)=\frac{p_g^a(s)}{q_g(s)},\qquad a\in\{A,B\}.
\]
The ratio is defined only for \(q_g(s)>0\), which includes every realized seed set. This ratio says how much more often the target would choose a seed set than the experiment does. It weights the entire village response, including spillovers. It is not the inverse probability that an individual resident is treated.
The importance-weighted value and contrast estimators are
\[
\widehat V_{\mathrm{HT}}(p^a)
=\frac1M\sum_g w_g^a(S_g)Y_g^{\mathrm{obs}},
\qquad
\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{HT}}
=\frac1M\sum_g\{w_g^A(S_g)-w_g^B(S_g)\}Y_g^{\mathrm{obs}}.
\tag{4}\]
Here HT emphasizes the same design-based cancellation used in L02, although the weight now contains a target-policy probability in its numerator.

Proposition 1 (Unbiased evaluation of a fixed stochastic policy) Under the stated consistency and support conditions, \(\mathbb E_q\{\widehat V_{\mathrm{HT}}(p^a)\}=V_M(p^a)\) and \(\mathbb E_q(\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{HT}})=\Delta_M(A,B)\). The subscript \(q\) denotes randomness under the experimental seed-selection design, with graphs and potential outcomes held fixed.


Proof. For each village,
\[
\mathbb E_q[w_g^a(S_g)Y_g^{\mathrm{obs}}]
=\sum_{s:q_g(s)>0}q_g(s)
\frac{p_g^a(s)}{q_g(s)}Y_g(s)
=\sum_s p_g^a(s)Y_g(s).
\]
Support coverage justifies the last equality. Averaging over villages estimates the policy value; subtracting the two identities estimates the contrast. Independence across villages is useful for variance analysis but is not needed for this expectation calculation if the correct marginal design probabilities are used.

On the star, suppose only uniform seeding was used. To evaluate one-hop seeding, the center receives weight \(3\) and each leaf weight \(1/3\). The weighted outcome is therefore \(12\) when the center is selected and \(2/3\) otherwise. Its expectation is \((1/4)12+(3/4)(2/3)=7/2\), the one-hop value. The counterfactual policy is evaluated without pretending that we observed the same village under a second seed.
The policy contrast uses contributions \(8\) at the center and \(-4/3\) at a leaf. Their expectation is one. A single contribution is a noisy estimate; the unbiasedness statement concerns repetitions of the experiment, and precision requires enough independent villages.


Why retain seed identities when strategies were randomized?
An experiment might first randomize a strategy label \(R_g\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\rho)\), with \(R_g=1\) selecting policy \(A\) and \(R_g=0\) selecting \(B\), then draw the seed set from that policy. After averaging over the label, the seed-set distribution is
\[
q_g(s)=\rho p_g^A(s)+(1-\rho)p_g^B(s),
\qquad 0<\rho<1.
\tag{5}\]
An ordinary arm-based HT contribution is
\[
T_g^{\mathrm{label}}
=\left\{\frac{R_g}{\rho}
-\frac{1-R_g}{1-\rho}\right\}Y_g^{\mathrm{obs}}.
\]
Its expectation is the village-specific policy contrast. But a seed set often could have been generated by either strategy. The label retains random variation that does not matter for the outcome once the seed set is known. Bayes’ rule gives
\[
\mathbb P(R_g=1\mid S_g=s)
=\frac{\rho p_g^A(s)}{q_g(s)}.
\]
Because the outcome depends only on \(s\), conditioning the label-based contribution on that set yields
\[
\mathbb E_q[T_g^{\mathrm{label}}\mid S_g]
=\frac{p_g^A(S_g)-p_g^B(S_g)}{q_g(S_g)}
Y_g^{\mathrm{obs}}.
\tag{6}\]
This is exactly the seed-set contribution in Equation 4. The law of total variance therefore proves that replacing the label contribution by this conditional expectation cannot increase its variance. For independent villages, the same comparison holds for their averages. This is a Rao–Blackwell argument relative to the specified label-HT estimator, not a universal efficiency ordering over every difference-in-means or normalized estimator.
The practical implication is simple: record which seeds were selected, not only which strategy was assigned. These details reveal how much the two policies agree about the realized intervention.
For the star with \(\rho=1/2\), the mixture chooses the center with probability \(1/2\) and each leaf with probability \(1/6\). The seed-set contrast contribution is \(4\) for the center and \(-2\) for a leaf. Its mean is one and its variance is \(\tfrac12(4^2)+\tfrac12(-2)^2-1^2=9\). The label-HT contribution has the same mean but variance \(39\). This is an exact calculation for the illustrative schedule, not a general numerical efficiency claim.


Normalization, support, and uncertainty
As in L02, a normalized estimator may stabilize random total weights:
\[
\widehat V_{\mathrm H}(p^a)
=\frac{\sum_g w_g^a(S_g)Y_g^{\mathrm{obs}}}
{\sum_g w_g^a(S_g)},
\qquad
\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm H}
=\widehat V_{\mathrm H}(p^A)-\widehat V_{\mathrm H}(p^B).
\tag{7}\]
Under full target support, each weight has expectation one, so the denominator fluctuates around \(M\). The ratio need not be exactly unbiased; a zero denominator must also be handled. Normalization changes the estimator, not which unobserved seed sets the experiment can inform.
The two policy estimates use the same villages. Their covariance is part of the uncertainty of the contrast. To see this directly, define the signed contribution \(D_g=\{w_g^A(S_g)-w_g^B(S_g)\}Y_g^{\mathrm{obs}}\). Under independent village assignments,
\[
\operatorname{Var}_q(\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{HT}})
=\frac1{M^2}\sum_g
\left[
\sum_{s:q_g(s)>0}
\frac{\{p_g^A(s)-p_g^B(s)\}^2Y_g(s)^2}{q_g(s)}
-\Delta_g^2
\right],
\tag{8}\]
where \(\Delta_g=\sum_s\{p_g^A(s)-p_g^B(s)\}Y_g(s)\). The difference of policy probabilities appears inside the square. Adding two separate value variances would discard the covariance that produces this expression.
For fixed, potentially heterogeneous villages, let \(s_D^2=(M-1)^{-1}\sum_g(D_g-\overline D)^2\) with \(\overline D=M^{-1}\sum_gD_g\). Independence gives
\[
\mathbb E_q\left[\frac{s_D^2}{M}\right]
=\operatorname{Var}_q(\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{HT}})
+\frac{\sum_g\{\Delta_g-\Delta_M(A,B)\}^2}{M(M-1)}.
\]
Thus the familiar sample-variance calculation is conservative in expectation in this setting; between-village contrast heterogeneity contributes an extra term. It is not an exact estimate of the assignment variance, nor does conservativeness in expectation alone justify a normal confidence interval. An appropriate many-village approximation and control of influential contributions are still needed. Counting thousands of residents does not create thousands of independent village-level experiments.
Under an explicitly stated iid-village sampling framework, full target support and finite second moments give the usual ratio expansion when the denominators converge to their positive expectations. The leading Hájek contrast fluctuation instead uses \(w^A(Y-V_A)-w^B(Y-V_B)\), where \(V_A,V_B\) are the corresponding population policy values. This again requires the covariance between policy estimates. It also changes the source of uncertainty by treating villages as a sample from a larger population rather than conditioning on the particular graphs.
The mixture design in Equation 5 bounds \(w_g^A\) by \(1/\rho\) and \(w_g^B\) by \(1/(1-\rho)\). A policy evaluated from an unrelated design can have much larger weights. Inspect the distribution of signed contributions, not just the average weight. Rare seed sets with large outcomes can dominate precision.
There is a subtle support distinction. Estimating both policy values requires coverage of their combined support. Estimating only their unnormalized contrast requires coverage wherever \(p_g^A(s)\ne p_g^B(s)\): unobserved sets with equal probabilities cancel. For example, with \(p^A=(.4,.2,.4)\), \(p^B=(.2,.4,.4)\), and \(q=(.5,.5,0)\), the identifiable contrast is \(.2Y(s_1)-.2Y(s_2)\), although neither complete policy value is identified. Separate Hájek normalization would divide each observable weighted mean by a quantity converging to \(.6\) across independent copies of this three-set setup, and generally would not recover that contrast. The weaker support argument applies to the signed, unnormalized estimator, not automatically to ratios.
Finally, evaluation of a fixed policy is not the same problem as learning which policy to deploy. Selecting a rule because it has the largest estimated value and reporting that estimate as if the rule were prespecified introduces selection bias. Independent evaluation villages or a suitable policy-learning analysis are needed. Splitting residents within a village does not, by itself, remove the dependence created by diffusion.

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
section: Policy evaluation when we observe a panel
text:
Policy evaluation when we observe a panel
The seeding problem asks what would happen under a different distribution over actions, using a known experiment to connect observed outcomes to that policy. Now change the information available. A city introduces a policy, a firm changes a practice, or a school adopts a program. We observe outcomes before and after adoption and observe other units over the same periods, but we do not necessarily know a credible randomization distribution for adoption. Can repeated observations supply the missing comparison?
A panel is a collection of units observed over time. Index units by \(i=1,\ldots,N\) and periods by \(t=1,\ldots,T\). Let \(Z_{it}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate treatment, and let \(Y_{it}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) be the observed outcome. Initially, assume that the outcome depends on the unit’s current treatment rather than its past treatment history or other units’ assignments. We can then write potential outcomes \(Y_{it}(0)\) and \(Y_{it}(1)\), with \(Y_{it}^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_{it}(Z_{it})\). We will return to treatment histories and spillovers before applying this formulation.
The object of interest is not necessarily the effect on all units in every period. Define the sets of untreated and treated cells by \[
\mathcal O=\{(i,t):Z_{it}=0\},
\qquad
\mathcal T=\{(i,t):Z_{it}=1\}.
\] For a nonempty \(\mathcal T\), consider the average effect on the units and periods actually treated: \[
\tau_{\mathcal T}
=\frac{1}{|\mathcal T|}
\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal T}
\{Y_{it}(1)-Y_{it}(0)\}.
\tag{9}\] Each treated cell receives equal weight; an average over units, cohorts, or event times would be a different target and should be defined accordingly. All the \(Y_{it}(1)\) appearing here are observed. The problem is to recover the untreated outcomes for these same cells.
This gives a useful rearrangement of the data. Form an \(N\)-by-\(T\) matrix of untreated potential outcomes. An untreated cell is observed, while a treated cell is missing. The observed treated outcome is not an observation of that missing entry: it belongs to a different potential-outcome matrix. The causal question becomes a matrix-completion problem, but changing its description does not supply an identification assumption.

What a before-and-after comparison needs
Suppose one unit adopts between periods 2 and 3. Its change in outcome mixes the policy’s effect with anything that would have changed without the policy. Difference-in-differences uses the change among untreated comparison units to account for the latter.
Let \(\overline Y_{\mathrm{tr},t}\) and \(\overline Y_{\mathrm{co},t}\) denote the observed averages for the treated and control groups in period \(t\). A two-period DID estimator is \[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DID}}
=(\overline Y_{\mathrm{tr},3}
  -\overline Y_{\mathrm{tr},2})
-(\overline Y_{\mathrm{co},3}
  -\overline Y_{\mathrm{co},2}).
\tag{10}\] The identifying comparison concerns what would have happened without treatment: the mean untreated change in the treated group must equal the mean untreated change in the controls. Equality of their outcome values is not required. Conversely, similar pretreatment values alone do not imply that their untreated changes would agree.
Why might DID fail while the rest of the panel still be useful? Different units may respond differently to common changes: a national demand shift may help one industry and hurt another. The following deliberately noiseless example isolates that issue. There are two never-treated controls and one unit treated only in the final period:

Suppose the treated unit’s untreated trajectory is twice A’s trajectory plus B’s trajectory. The first two entries satisfy this relation: \(4=2(1)+2\) and \(5=2(2)+1\). If the same relation continues, the missing entry is \(2(3)+0=6\). If the observed treated outcome is 8, the treatment effect is 2. Equal-weight controls instead average 1.5 in every period. DID therefore predicts no untreated change for the treated unit, imputes 5, and estimates an effect of 3. The problem is not a shortage of time observations in principle: it is the assumption that the unweighted control change is the right comparison.
The relation used to obtain 6 needs justification. It is not guaranteed because it fits two observations. We next express precisely what it means to assume that a small collection of stable patterns governs the panel.

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
section: Low rank means shared patterns with different responses
text:
Low rank means shared patterns with different responses
Imagine that untreated outcomes reflect a small number of common time patterns. One might represent national demand, another the relative cost of energy. Units have different sensitivities to these patterns. Let \(\mathbf u_i\in\mathbb R^r\) collect unit \(i\)’s sensitivities, called loadings, and let \(\mathbf f_t\in\mathbb R^r\) collect the common factors in period \(t\). The interaction component of the mean is \[
L_{it}=\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf f_t
      =\sum_{k=1}^r u_{ik}f_{tk}.
\tag{11}\] The loadings do not receive a time index: their stability is part of the model. Factors may vary over time without following a linear or smooth trend. A single factor can increase, fall, and increase again, while units respond with different magnitudes and even different signs.
Stack the row vectors \(\mathbf u_i^\top\) into an \(N\)-by-\(r\) matrix \(\mathbf U\) and \(\mathbf f_t^\top\) into a \(T\)-by-\(r\) matrix \(\mathbf F\). Then \[
\mathbf L=\mathbf U\mathbf F^\top,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf L)\le r.
\tag{12}\] Every row of \(\mathbf L\) is a linear combination of the same \(r\) time patterns, and every column is a linear combination of the same \(r\) loading patterns across units. Low rank is therefore a restriction in both directions, not merely a claim that outcomes are highly correlated.
The factors need not have unique scientific names. Replacing \(\mathbf U\) by \(\mathbf U\mathbf H\) and \(\mathbf F\) by \(\mathbf F\mathbf H^{-\top}\), for an invertible \(r\)-by-\(r\) matrix \(\mathbf H\), leaves \(\mathbf L\) unchanged. Identifying a counterfactual mean can be possible without identifying a uniquely labeled set of latent mechanisms.
For policy evaluation, separate persistent unit differences and common time changes from the interaction component. A working model is \[
Y_{it}(0)
=\underbrace{\alpha_i+\delta_t+L_{it}}_{M_{it}^{0}}
+\varepsilon_{it},
\qquad
\mathbf L=\mathbf U\mathbf F^\top.
\tag{13}\] Here \(M_{it}^{0}\) is the systematic untreated mean and \(\varepsilon_{it}\) is a residual. The additive terms allow, for example, one city to have a persistently higher outcome while all cities experience a common period shock. The interaction terms allow the same shock to have different effects across cities. This is the interactive-fixed-effects perspective developed in the panel literature (Bai 2009).
Three distinctions matter. First, the mean is modeled as low dimensional; independent measurement noise will generally make the realized outcome matrix full rank. Second, the rank bound \(r\) applies to \(\mathbf L\). The full mean matrix \(\mathbf M^0\) has rank at most \(r+2\), since each additive component contributes at most one. Third, this is now an outcome-model argument. Without a randomized adoption design, the model and the way treated cells differ from untreated cells must do work that randomization previously did for us.
Here a mean refers to an expectation over residual variation, holding the systematic components fixed. Mean-zero residuals before conditioning on treatment need not remain mean zero among treated cells. A causal analysis needs restrictions on that selection as well as on the rank of the signal; we will make their role explicit in the estimator’s error decomposition.

Which missing entries are determined?
Return to the noiseless example, now imposing rank two directly on its untreated mean matrix. The first two control rows are independent. Their first two coordinates determine the coefficients of the treated row: \[
a+2b=4,\qquad 2a+b=5
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=2,\quad b=1.
\] Rank two says the third row stays in their span, which determines the final entry as 6. Both the structural restriction and the observed arrangement are essential.
For a general noiseless matrix, reorder rows into controls followed by treated units and columns into pre- and post-treatment periods. Write \[
\mathbf M^0=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf A&\mathbf B\\
\mathbf C&\mathbf D
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{14}\] We observe control outcomes before and after treatment, \(\mathbf A\) and \(\mathbf B\), and treated-unit outcomes before treatment, \(\mathbf C\). The block \(\mathbf D\) is missing.

Proposition 2 (Completing a noiseless block) If \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf M^0)=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf A)=r_0\), then \[
\mathbf D=\mathbf C\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf B,
\tag{15}\] where \(\mathbf A^\dagger\) is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.


Proof. Stack the two observed pretreatment blocks vertically to form \(\mathbf K=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf A\\\mathbf C\end{pmatrix}\). Its columns have rank \(r_0\) and span the columns of the complete matrix. Thus the post-treatment columns can be written \(\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf B\\\mathbf D\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf K\mathbf H\) for some coefficient matrix \(\mathbf H\). Reading its upper and lower blocks gives \(\mathbf B=\mathbf A\mathbf H\) and \(\mathbf D=\mathbf C\mathbf H\). Also, \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf K)
=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf A)\) implies that each row of \(\mathbf C\) lies in the row space of \(\mathbf A\). Thus \(\mathbf C=\mathbf C\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf A\). Substituting, \[
\mathbf C\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf B
=\mathbf C\mathbf A^\dagger\mathbf A\mathbf H
=\mathbf C\mathbf H=\mathbf D.
\]

The rank condition says that the controls in the pretreatment periods reveal all the directions needed elsewhere in the matrix. It is a form of overlap in latent structure. A policy-responsive group cannot have an additional untreated pattern that is completely invisible in the observed comparison data.
Low rank alone does not supply that overlap. Suppose the three observed entries of a two-by-two matrix are zero and only its bottom-right entry is missing: \[
\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&d\end{pmatrix}.
\] Every value of \(d\) is compatible with rank at most one; restricting rank to exactly one still allows every nonzero \(d\). Nothing observed tells us how large the missing entry is. Even when completion is unique, it may be unstable: for a rank-one matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) with \(a\ne0\), the missing value is \(d=bc/a\). A small error in a nearly zero \(a\) can produce a large prediction error.

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
section: Estimating a mean matrix from noisy untreated cells
text:
Estimating a mean matrix from noisy untreated cells
In a realistic panel, exact algebraic completion is too brittle. Untreated observations contain noise, rank is unknown, and adoption may create a staircase of missing cells rather than a single rectangle. We need a method that rewards fitting untreated observations while discouraging elaborate patterns supported only by noise.
Without a complexity restriction, minimizing squared errors over \(\mathcal O\) reproduces every observed untreated value and leaves every missing entry arbitrary. A rank constraint would connect these entries, but choosing a rank and solving the resulting factorization problem can be difficult. The nuclear norm provides a convex alternative.
Let \(\sigma_k(\mathbf L)\) be the singular values of a matrix, the nonnegative strengths of its orthogonal row-column patterns. Its rank counts nonzero singular values; its nuclear norm adds their magnitudes: \[
\|\mathbf L\|_*=\sum_{k=1}^{\min(N,T)}\sigma_k(\mathbf L).
\tag{16}\] Penalizing this sum encourages weak patterns to vanish and strong patterns to shrink. It is not a penalty on the absolute values of individual cells. Changing a missing cell can change the singular values and therefore change the penalty even though that cell has no observed-data loss.
A matrix-completion estimator developed for causal panels by Athey et al. (2021) solves the following optimization problem. Write \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_N)\) and \(\delta=(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_T)\) for the vectors of additive effects: \[
(\widehat\alpha,\widehat\delta,\widehat{\mathbf L})
\in\arg\min_{\alpha,\delta,\mathbf L}
\left[
\frac{1}{2|\mathcal O|}
\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal O}
\{Y_{it}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\alpha_i-\delta_t-L_{it}\}^2
+\lambda\|\mathbf L\|_*
\right],
\tag{17}\] where \(\lambda\ge0\) controls regularization. The factor of two merely sets the scale of \(\lambda\). The prediction is \(\widehat M_{it}^{0}=\widehat\alpha_i+\widehat\delta_t+\widehat L_{it}\). An additive normalization, such as \(\sum_i\alpha_i=0\), can fix the redundancy between unit and time intercepts; the fitted sum is the object we need.
The additive effects are unpenalized so that a large persistent difference between units need not be shrunk merely to achieve a simpler interaction matrix. Crucially, the summation uses only untreated cells. Including treated outcomes in this same loss would invite the model to explain the policy’s effect as part of the untreated signal. Doing that legitimately would require additional restrictions on the treatment-effect component.

What the penalty does computationally
The complete-data analogue makes the mechanism transparent. If a matrix \(\mathbf R\) is fully observed and additive effects have been removed, consider \[
\min_{\mathbf L}
\frac12\|\mathbf R-\mathbf L\|_F^2+\kappa\|\mathbf L\|_*,
\tag{18}\] where \(\|\cdot\|_F^2\) adds squared entries and \(\kappa\ge0\). Write a singular-value decomposition \(\mathbf R=\mathbf P\operatorname{diag}(s_k)\mathbf Q^\top\). The optimizer retains these singular-vector directions and replaces each \(s_k\) by \((s_k-\kappa)_+=\max(s_k-\kappa,0)\). Along one such direction, the remaining optimization is simply \(\min_{\ell\ge0}\frac12(s_k-\ell)^2+\kappa\ell\): an interior solution has \(\ell=s_k-\kappa\), and otherwise the minimum is at zero. Thus weak directions disappear instead of being fitted exactly.
With missing entries we cannot take one decomposition of a complete observed matrix. Soft-impute algorithms repeatedly fill missing entries with current predictions and shrink the resulting singular values, updating until convergence (Mazumder, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2010). Missing entries are working predictions, not new observations. A one-time replacement of missing values by zero followed by an ordinary SVD does not generally solve the masked fitting problem.


Turning predictions into an effect estimate
Average the differences between observed treated outcomes and predicted untreated means: \[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{MC}}
=\frac{1}{|\mathcal T|}
\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal T}
\{Y_{it}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\widehat M_{it}^{0}\}.
\tag{19}\] This formula is simple, but its error exposes two different tasks. Under Equation 13, \[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{MC}}-\tau_{\mathcal T}
=\frac{1}{|\mathcal T|}
\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal T}(M_{it}^{0}-\widehat M_{it}^{0})
+\frac{1}{|\mathcal T|}
\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal T}\varepsilon_{it}.
\tag{20}\] The first term is error in estimating untreated means. The second is the average untreated residual for the treated cells. Even knowing the mean matrix exactly would not reveal each unobserved realization of \(Y_{it}(0)\). To estimate the realized finite-panel effect precisely, we need that residual average to be small or an uncertainty analysis that accounts for it.
A condition such as mean-zero residuals given the signal and the treatment pattern helps prevent selection on unexplained shocks; suitable independence or weak dependence then makes averaging informative. If cities adopt precisely when their unmodeled outcome shocks worsen, the residual average need not be zero. Better matrix fitting cannot repair that selection automatically. Alternatively, an analyst might target an average effect in conditional expectation under a stated model. That is a legitimate change of estimand, but not a reason to equate a predicted mean with an individual missing potential outcome.


Choosing complexity and checking the comparison
Larger \(\lambda\) more strongly favors fewer and smaller interaction patterns; too much regularization misses real heterogeneity, while too little can fit noise. Choose it using untreated outcomes only. A basic cross-validation procedure withholds some untreated cells, fits on the rest, and compares predictions with the withheld values over a grid of penalties. Refit the chosen model using all available untreated cells.
The arrangement of holdouts matters. Predicting randomly scattered entries with neighbors observed on both sides is easier than predicting a long post-adoption block. In addition to ordinary masking, examine pseudo-adoption dates or withheld time blocks that resemble the intended extrapolation, while leaving enough controls and periods to estimate the model. This is a diagnostic design choice, not a theorem that cross-validation identifies causal effects. If final control-period outcomes will be available for the retrospective analysis, they may legitimately inform its fit; forecasting before those periods occur is a different information problem.
Inspect sensitivity to penalty strength, donor units, the pretreatment window, and the treatment date. Large changes reveal dependence on particular extrapolations. Good held-out predictions support the model in regions where outcomes can be checked; they do not test whether a new unobserved shock affects only the treated cells.

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
section: What must be checked before calling the result causal?
text:
What must be checked before calling the result causal?
Panel structure supplies repeated measurements, not randomized adoption. The scientific justification should specify which untreated comparison can travel across units and time, and why treatment does not select residual changes left out of that comparison. The recovery assumptions also need enough untreated information in relevant periods and enough pretreatment information for relevant units. If everyone adopts and no post-adoption controls remain, unrestricted future factors cannot generally be learned from these data alone.
The indexing of potential outcomes must fit the policy. A treatment may have effects that accumulate, persist after withdrawal, or begin in anticipation. With irreversible adoption, one can instead index outcomes by adoption date \(g\) and compare \(Y_{it}(g)\) with the never-adopted outcome \(Y_{it}(\infty)\). No anticipation allows pre-adoption observations to inform the latter. This formulation permits duration-dependent treatment effects; it does not make a current-treatment-only model correct. Staggered adoption then produces different missing blocks for different cohorts. Specify the cohort-period effects being averaged, and do not use already-treated observations as untreated controls without additional assumptions.
The units must also be chosen with spillovers in mind. If a city’s policy changes outcomes in neighboring control cities, their observed outcomes need not be observations of the counterfactual world being imputed. The interference issues of L05 have not disappeared; a useful panel method must either rule them out, model them, or redefine the comparison.
Finally, prediction and inference are separate achievements. A small matrix-reconstruction error does not by itself produce a confidence interval for a particular treated-cell average. A small error averaged over the whole panel can even hide a large error in a small target block. Uncertainty can include counterfactual prediction error, regularization bias, the unobserved residual average, and estimation of weights or factors. Resampling cells independently ignores serial dependence within units. Unit-level resampling is more appropriate under independent-unit models, but few treated units and dependence between units create further limitations. Placebo comparisons are informative diagnostics; they are exact randomization tests only when a suitable assignment mechanism actually justifies those permutations.
For contrast, Athey and Imbens (2022) study panels from an explicitly design-based perspective in which adoption dates are randomly assigned. That returns uncertainty to the randomization distribution and provides a different justification from assuming a low-rank untreated mean. One should say which argument is being used rather than blending them.

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
text:
Synthesis
Both halves of this lecture begin by specifying an intervention and its missing comparison. In seeding experiments, the policy is a distribution over seed sets, and known randomization can identify its value through reweighting. In a nonrandomized panel, repeated observations can reveal shared patterns from which to construct an untreated comparison, but only if those patterns remain informative where the counterfactuals are missing.
The common question is not whether an estimator has an appealing name. It is what connects the observed outcomes to the proposed intervention. Support in the experiment and informative factor variation in the panel both limit extrapolation, although they are different mathematical conditions. A useful analysis makes that connection explicit, then separates estimating the comparison from quantifying its uncertainty.

title: L07: Policy Evaluation and Panel Data
text:
Further reading
Chin, Eckles, and Ugander (2022) develop the seeding-policy evaluation framework. The seed-set calculations above connect it to the change-of-distribution argument behind importance sampling and to Rao–Blackwellization. Their applications also illustrate why the relative performance of targeting rules is an empirical question, not a conclusion that follows from centrality alone.
Athey et al. (2021) connect causal-panel imputation to matrix completion and to prediction across units and across time. Bai (2009) supplies earlier foundations for panels with interactive fixed effects, while Mazumder, Hastie, and Tibshirani (2010) develops the spectral regularization algorithms.
Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010) develop synthetic controls for comparative case studies. Arkhangelsky et al. (2021) combine unit and time weighting with difference-in-differences. Their inferential analysis, and Chernozhukov et al. (2023) on inference after low-rank estimation, show why uncertainty requires more than an accurate fitted matrix.
Athey and Imbens (2022) offer the contrasting design-based treatment of staggered adoption. Their separation of assignment assumptions from restrictions on anticipation and treatment history is useful even when one ultimately chooses a model-based analysis.

title: Notation
text:
Units, samples, and populations

\(N\) is the number of units in the finite experimental population, indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,N\).
\(n\) is the sample size in explicitly stated i.i.d. superpopulation or observational-sampling arguments. Do not silently replace the finite experimental population indexed by \(N\) with an i.i.d. sample indexed by \(n\).
\(X_i\) is the vector of pretreatment covariates for unit \(i\); \(\mathbf X\) collects these vectors.
A target population beyond the experimental units is described explicitly. Do not use “ATE” without making its target population clear.

text:
Treatments, assignments, and exposures

\(Z_i\in\{0,1\}\) is unit \(i\)’s treatment assignment, with \(1\) denoting treatment and \(0\) control. The assignment vector is \(\mathbf Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N)\).
\(N_1=\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i\) and \(N_0=N-N_1\) are the realized treatment-arm sizes.
\(\mathcal Z\) is the support of the experimental design, the set of assignment vectors with positive probability.
When units are partitioned into \(H\) design strata or blocks, \(h=1,\ldots,H\) indexes the strata, \(N_h\) is the stratum size, and \(N_{1h}\) and \(N_{0h}\) are its treatment-arm sizes.
crumbs: 12  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Potential outcomes and observed outcomes

\(Y_i(z)\) is the potential outcome for unit \(i\) under treatment level \(z\in\{0,1\}\).
\(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_i(Z_i)=Z_iY_i(1)+(1-Z_i)Y_i(0)\) is the observed outcome when SUTVA and consistency hold.
\(\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\) is unit \(i\)’s treatment effect.
crumbs: 12  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Estimands and estimators

\(\overline Y(z)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i(z)\) is the finite-population mean potential outcome under treatment level \(z\).
\(\tau=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\tau_i=\overline Y(1)-\overline Y(0)\) is the finite-population average treatment effect. Qualify population and conditional versions with a subscript or argument, such as \(\tau_P\), \(\tau(x)\), or \(\tau_g\).
In a stated superpopulation, \(\tau_P=\mathbb E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\}\) denotes the population ATE. For a measurable covariate subset \(A\), \(\tau_A=\mathbb E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X\in A\}\) is the ATE in the restricted target population. For a nonnegative tilting function \(h\), \(\tau_h=\mathbb E[h(X)\{Y(1)-Y(0)\}]/\mathbb E\{h(X)\}\) is the ATE in the corresponding tilted target population.
A hat denotes an estimator, a random function of the assignment and observed outcomes. Its value at the realized data is an estimate.
\(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}\) denotes the treated-minus-control difference in observed means.
\(\widehat\mu_{z,\mathrm{HT}}\) and \(\widehat\mu_{z,\mathrm{H}}\) denote, respectively, the Horvitz–Thompson and Hájek estimators of \(\overline Y(z)\). The corresponding treatment-effect estimators are \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}=\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{HT}}-
\widehat\mu_{0,\mathrm{HT}}\) and \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{H}}=\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{H}}-
\widehat\mu_{0,\mathrm{H}}\).
\(\widehat\mu_\lambda\) denotes a member of the Trotter–Tukey affine normalization family, with Horvitz–Thompson at \(\lambda=0\) and Hájek at \(\lambda=1\). \(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{AN}}\) denotes the adaptively normalized fixed-point estimator.
\(\overline X=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\) is the finite-population covariate mean. Center covariates at \(\overline X\) when writing regression-adjusted treatment effects.
\(\widehat\tau_X=\overline X_1^{\mathrm{obs}}-
\overline X_0^{\mathrm{obs}}\) denotes realized covariate mean imbalance.
In superpopulation arguments, \(m_z(x)=\mathbb E\{Y(z)\mid X=x\}\) denotes the conditional potential-outcome mean for arm \(z\). In design-based arguments, the same symbol may denote a working outcome prediction; distinguish the population conditional mean, a function fixed before assignment, and a function fitted using realized outcomes.
\(\widehat\mu_{z,\mathrm{AIPW}}\) denotes the prediction-plus-IPW-correction estimator of \(\overline Y(z)\), and \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{AIPW}}=\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{AIPW}}-
\widehat\mu_{0,\mathrm{AIPW}}\).
crumbs: 12  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Assignment and sampling probabilities

\(\mathbb P_Z\), \(\mathbb E_Z\), \(\operatorname{Var}_Z\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}_Z\) refer to probability under the assignment design, holding the finite population and all potential outcomes fixed.
\(\pi_i=\mathbb P_Z(Z_i=1)\) is unit \(i\)’s marginal treatment probability.
When both treatment states appear symmetrically, use \(\pi_i(z)=\mathbb P_Z(Z_i=z)\), so that \(\pi_i(1)=\pi_i\) and \(\pi_i(0)=1-\pi_i\).
Use \(p\) for a common Bernoulli assignment probability.
In observational or superpopulation arguments, \(e(x)=\mathbb P(Z=1\mid X=x)\) is the propensity score. Introduce the change of framework explicitly; do not use \(e(x)\) as though it were the known finite-population design probability \(\pi_i\).
crumbs: 12  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Finite-population and superpopulation operators

For \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(S_z^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\{Y_i(z)-\overline Y(z)\}^2\) is the finite-population variance of potential outcomes.
\(S_\tau^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(\tau_i-\tau)^2\) is the finite-population variance of unit-level treatment effects.
Within stratum \(h\), use \(\tau_h\), \(S_{zh}^2\), and \(S_{\tau h}^2\) for the stratum ATE and the corresponding finite-population variances.
\(s_z^2\) is the usual sample variance of observed outcomes within realized arm \(z\).
Unsubscripted probabilistic expectations such as \(\mathbb E\) refer to a stated superpopulation or statistical model, not to the assignment design.
crumbs: 12  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Networks and interference

Under interference, \(Y_i(\mathbf z)\) is unit \(i\)’s potential outcome under the full assignment vector \(\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N\), and \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_i(\mathbf Z)\). The two-outcome notation \(Y_i(z)\) applies when other units’ assignments do not affect unit \(i\).
\(\mathcal N_i\) is the known interference neighborhood of unit \(i\), including \(i\) unless explicitly stated otherwise; \(d_i=|\mathcal N_i|\). For a directed interference network, \(j\in\mathcal N_i\) means that treatment of \(j\) may affect the outcome of \(i\).
\(\tau_{\mathrm G}=N^{-1}\sum_i\{Y_i(\mathbf 1_N)-Y_i(\mathbf 0_N)\}\) is the global average treatment effect (GATE), also called the total treatment effect (TTE) in the interference literature. It is an average over units even when called a total effect.
\(E_i=f_i(\mathbf Z)\) is the exposure induced by a prespecified mapping. When the mapping is sufficient, \(y_i(e)\) denotes the common potential outcome under assignments with exposure label \(e\). When used for exposure probabilities, \(\pi_i(e)=\mathbb P_Z(E_i=e)\) and \(\pi_{ij}(e,e')=\mathbb P_Z(E_i=e,E_j=e')\); the argument denotes an exposure label rather than a unit’s own treatment state.
\(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_K\}\) is a partition into clusters, \(c(i)\) is the index of unit \(i\)’s cluster, and \(W_k\) is cluster \(k\)’s treatment. Cluster-constant assignment means \(Z_i=W_{c(i)}\). \(k_i(\mathcal C)\) counts the clusters intersecting \(\mathcal N_i\).
A low-order outcome model has maximum interaction order \(\beta\) and subset collection \(\mathcal S_i^\beta
=\{S\subseteq\mathcal N_i:|S|\le\beta\}\), including the empty set. The feature vector \(\mathbf v_i(\mathbf z)\) contains the monomials \(\prod_{j\in S}z_j\) for these subsets, with the empty product equal to one.
\(\mathbf c_i\) collects the coefficients in \(Y_i(\mathbf z)=\mathbf v_i(\mathbf z)^\top\mathbf c_i\). \(\mathbf a_i=\mathbf v_i(\mathbf 1_N)-\mathbf v_i(\mathbf 0_N)\) selects unit \(i\)’s contribution to the global contrast.
\(\mathbf M_i=\mathbb E_Z[
\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)\mathbf v_i(\mathbf Z)^\top]\) is the design second-moment matrix, and \(\mathbf M_i^\dagger\) is its Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. Define any fitted or empirical matrix separately.
crumbs: 12  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Stochastic policy evaluation

In network seeding examples, \(M\) is the number of villages or independent networks, indexed by \(g\). \(S_g\) is the selected seed set, and \(Y_g(s)\) is the village-level potential outcome under seed set \(s\).
\(p_g^a(s)\) is the seed-set probability under target policy \(a\); \(q_g(s)\) is its probability under the actual experimental design. \(\mathbb E_q\) and \(\operatorname{Var}_q\) hold the villages, graphs, and potential outcomes fixed and average over this design.
\(V_M(p)=M^{-1}\sum_g\sum_s p_g(s)Y_g(s)\) is a policy’s value averaged over the fixed villages. \(\Delta_M(A,B)=V_M(p^A)-V_M(p^B)\) is the policy-value contrast. State any alternative village or resident weights.
crumbs: 12  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Panel data and matrices

Panel units are indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,N\) and periods by \(t=1,\ldots,T\). \(Z_{it}\) denotes treatment. The notation \(Y_{it}(z)\) presumes that a contemporaneous treatment indicator adequately describes the intervention; introduce treatment-history notation when anticipation or carryover matters.
\(\mathcal O=\{(i,t):Z_{it}=0\}\) is the set of observed untreated cells, and \(\mathcal T=\{(i,t):Z_{it}=1\}\) is the treated set. The complete matrix of observed outcomes is not the matrix of untreated potential outcomes: entries of the latter are missing on \(\mathcal T\).
\(\tau_{\mathcal T}=|\mathcal T|^{-1}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal T}
\{Y_{it}(1)-Y_{it}(0)\}\) averages effects over the specified treated cells.
\(M_{it}^0\) is the systematic untreated outcome in \(Y_{it}(0)=M_{it}^0+\varepsilon_{it}\). In a factor model, \(M_{it}^0=\alpha_i+\delta_t+L_{it}\) with \(\mathbf L=\mathbf U\mathbf F^\top\) and \(L_{it}=\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf f_t\). \(r\) denotes the rank bound on \(\mathbf L\), not necessarily on the full mean matrix after adding fixed effects.
\(\|\mathbf L\|_*=\sum_j\sigma_j(\mathbf L)\) is the nuclear norm, the sum of the singular values. Distinguish this penalty from a hard constraint on the number of nonzero singular values.

Always subscript probability, expectation, and variance when more than one source of randomness is in play.

Project 1
The three course projects are completed in groups of 2-4 students. Each project has three parts: a proposal 1-pager, an in-class presentation, and a write-up.
The proposal 1-pager is a one-page PDF uploaded to Canvas. It should state the project topic—including the paper selected for Project 1 or Project 2—list the group members, and give a one-paragraph summary of what the group intends to investigate.
Both proposal 1-pagers and write-ups are due at 11:59 p.m. ET on the dates shown below.
Choose a paper roughly corresponding to L01–L04, study its contribution closely, replicate its analysis, and consider possible extensions. The paper choice must be approved by the instructor before the group proceeds.

title: Projects
text:
Possible papers
The following papers are starting points rather than a closed list. They span the material in L01–L04 and vary in theoretical, computational, and empirical emphasis. In the proposal 1-pager, identify a tractable result, simulation, or empirical analysis to replicate and a specific extension or sensitivity analysis to investigate.

Randomization inference beyond the sharp null (L01). Caughey, Dafoe, Li, and Miratrix (2023), Randomisation Inference beyond the Sharp Null: Bounded Null Hypotheses and Quantiles of Individual Treatment Effects. Reproduce one of the proposed tests or bounds, then study its finite-sample behavior, computational demands, or sensitivity to the assignment design.
Estimated propensity scores and efficiency (L02). Hirano, Imbens, and Ridder (2003), Efficient Estimation of Average Treatment Effects Using the Estimated Propensity Score. Reconstruct the paper’s efficiency comparison and investigate when estimating rather than inserting a known propensity score helps in finite samples.
Adaptive normalization of inverse-probability weights (L02). Khan and Ugander (2023), Adaptive Normalization for IPW Estimation. Replicate the comparisons among Horvitz–Thompson, Hájek, and adaptively normalized estimators, then alter the assignment design, outcome structure, or nuisance estimation method.
Regression adjustment in randomized experiments (L02–L03). Lin (2013), Agnostic Notes on Regression Adjustments to Experimental Data: Reexamining Freedman’s Critique. Reproduce a central simulation or empirical comparison and examine the role of treatment–covariate interactions, imbalance, or unequal treatment allocation.
Rerandomization (L03). Morgan and Rubin (2012), Rerandomization to Improve Covariate Balance in Experiments. Implement the design and reproduce its balance or precision gains, then vary the acceptance rule, balance metric, covariate dimension, or analysis procedure.
Algorithmic covariate balancing (L03). Harshaw, Sävje, Spielman, and Zhang (2024), Balancing Covariates in Randomized Experiments with the Gram–Schmidt Walk Design. Implement a manageable part of the design and compare its balance–randomness tradeoff with complete randomization or rerandomization.
Limited overlap and optimal trimming (L04). Crump, Hotz, Imbens, and Mitnik (2009), Dealing with Limited Overlap in Estimation of Average Treatment Effects. Reproduce the trimming rule and a key simulation, then examine how trimming changes both precision and the population whose effect is being estimated.
Smooth trimming and post-trimming inference (L04). Yang and Ding (2018), Asymptotic Inference of Causal Effects with Observational Studies Trimmed by the Estimated Propensity Scores. Compare hard trimming with smooth weighting and study bootstrap inference or uncertainty from the design stage.
Heteroscedasticity-aware trimming (L04). Khan and Ugander (2025), Doubly Robust and Heteroscedasticity-Aware Sample Trimming for Causal Inference. Replicate a simulation or application, then compare propensity-only and conditional-variance-aware trimming under alternative forms of heteroscedasticity.
Regularizing extrapolation (L04). Arbour, Parikh, Niknam, Stuart, Rudolph, and Feller (2026), Regularizing Extrapolation in Causal Inference. Implement the proposed regularization and investigate the paper’s bias–bias–variance tradeoff as overlap, dimension, or the outcome model changes.

title: Projects
text:
Project 2
Choose a paper aligned with the material in L05–L07, study its contribution closely, replicate its analysis, and consider possible extensions. The paper choice must be approved by the instructor before the group proceeds.

Possible papers
The following papers are starting points rather than a closed list. They span interference, structural outcome models, policy evaluation, and panel data. As in Project 1, identify a tractable result, simulation, or empirical analysis to replicate and a specific extension or sensitivity analysis to investigate. If the original application uses unavailable data, a simulation or theoretical investigation can provide the basis for the project.

Testing interference (L05). Athey, Eckles, and Imbens (2018), Exact \(p\)-Values for Network Interference. Implement one conditional randomization test and reproduce its size and power under a specified interference model, then investigate how the choice of focal units, test statistic, or network structure affects its ability to detect spillovers.
Randomizing graph clusters (L05). Ugander and Yin (2023), Randomized Graph Cluster Randomization. Reproduce a comparison of fixed and randomized clustering, including the calculation or estimation of exposure probabilities, then investigate how graph structure, the clustering algorithm, or computational effort changes estimator variance and mean squared error.
Low-order interference models (L06). Cortez-Rodriguez, Eichhorn, and Yu (2023), Exploiting Neighborhood Interference with Low-Order Interactions under Unit Randomized Design. Implement the low-order estimator and reproduce a simulation comparison, then study the bias–variance tradeoff when the assumed interaction order is too small or unnecessarily large.
Combining outcome models and experimental design (L05–L06). Eichhorn, Khan, Ugander, and Yu (2026), Low-order Outcomes and Clustered Designs: Combining Design and Analysis for Causal Inference under Network Interference. Reproduce a pseudoinverse-estimator comparison across clusterings, then examine whether the proposed variance bounds select useful designs when the graph or outcome model changes.
Covariate adjustment under interference (L06). Wang and Li (2026), Covariate Adjustment Cannot Hurt: Treatment Effect Estimation under Interference with Low-Order Outcome Interactions. Compare the proposed adjustment with unadjusted estimation and ordinary regression adjustment, then investigate finite-sample precision and interval coverage as covariate informativeness, network density, or model misspecification changes.
Monotonicity and attributable effects (L06). Choi (2017), Estimation of Monotone Treatment Effects in Network Experiments. Implement a confidence-interval procedure for effects attributable to the realized treatment assignment, then study how its width and coverage depend on network information and the monotonicity assumption, including sensitivity to departures from that assumption.
Evaluating stochastic seeding policies (L07). Chin, Eckles, and Ugander (2022), Evaluating Stochastic Seeding Strategies in Networks. Reproduce a comparison of seeding strategies using the proposed policy-value estimators, then vary the diffusion model, network structure, or experimental assignment rule to study precision and overlap between policies.
Matrix completion for causal panels (L07). Athey, Bayati, Doudchenko, Imbens, and Khosravi (2021), Matrix Completion Methods for Causal Panel Data Models. Reproduce a counterfactual-prediction comparison, then investigate how latent rank, the pattern of treatment adoption, or the choice of regularization affects treatment-effect estimates. Distinguish prediction accuracy on observed cells from accuracy on treated cells.
Synthetic difference-in-differences (L07). Arkhangelsky, Athey, Hirshberg, Imbens, and Wager (2021), Synthetic Difference-in-Differences. Replicate a comparison with difference-in-differences and synthetic control, then investigate the role of unit and time weights as pretreatment history, latent trends, or the donor pool changes.
